  **16 citations across nine pages were rewritten to keys**, so the same paper is no longer said three different ways in three plugin help pages. A test fails on any reference bullet that is still a hand-written DOI link, and another on a malformed or supplementary DOI in the bibliography.

  **The `?` modal now renders like the browser.** It used Qt's own `setMarkdown`, which knows no MyST — so a plugin's help page showed `:::{note}`, `` {cite}`key` `` and raw LaTeX as literal text: precisely the defects fixed in the browser, in the window most readers actually open. One entry point (`chisurf/gui/widgets/tools/help_render.py`) now serves every widget that displays a help page — the `?` modal, AutoForm `info` sections, the LUT tool's README dialog — and falls back to Qt's Markdown only when rendering genuinely fails. Found by putting citations into the plugin help pages and then checking what the modal did with them, which is the only way this kind of gap surfaces.

* **Which parts of the reference sources have been mined, and when they are exhausted** ([pymol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)).

  ChiMOL is built by reading PyMOL's source and transcribing it -- the rule that has been right every time it was followed -- but nothing in the tree could say *which parts had already been read*. So the same file gets re-read by the next session, and "is the source exhausted?" had no answer. It does now: **14 files of 461** (3.0 %) across the layers the parity work actually reads. Nowhere near.

  **Editing the reference checkouts is now sanctioned, for the header only.** A `CHIMOL-REVIEWED` / `CHIMOL-TAKEN` / `CHIMOL-SKIPPED` / `CHIMOL-RECORD` block goes at the top of each file that has been read, so it is found by whoever opens the file rather than by whoever thinks to search the knowledge base. Never the code: a `git diff` inside the checkout must show insertions and **zero deletions**, which is what the 14 PyMOL files and 2 ChimeraX files stamped here do (87 insertions, 0 deletions).

  **`SKIPPED` is the half that pays.** "Read and deliberately not taken, for this reason" is the expensive knowledge -- without it the next session re-reads the file, reaches the same conclusion and pays again, which is exactly what `valence` cost. The markers carry, among others: `RepValence` blocked on bond orders, `ribbon_color` having no separate representation here, ChimeraX's shadow maps unbuilt, and its GL abstraction rejected in favour of driving PyOpenGL directly.

  **The markers are an index; this concept is the record.** `junk/` is gitignored and re-clonable, so a re-clone loses every marker and nothing else -- which is why each one points back at the OKF concept, and why the tool reports a fresh checkout as 0 %. `analysis/reference_coverage.py` measures it, with the denominator restricted to the directories that matter (PyMOL is ~3000 files, mostly build glue). 6 tests, which build their own miniature checkout so they run without the 132 MB one.

* **Correction, and why `valence` is not next** ([pymol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)).

  **The PyMOL checkout was never deleted.** The previous entry recorded that `junk/pymol-open-source` -- the tracker's stated authority on behaviour -- had been removed during this session. It had not: the directory was unreadable for a few minutes (most likely while another instance re-cloned it, and `clone.sh` skips what is already there) and is present and complete, `layer2/`, `modules/pymol/util.py` and all 819 records of `SettingInfo.h`. Corrected in the tracker, because a false statement in the durable layer is worse than no statement: the next session would have re-cloned 132 MB or, worse, transcribed from memory.

  **`valence` is blocked on data, not on drawing.** It is high on the appearance ranking and the algorithm transcribes cleanly -- `RepValence` builds a local frame from the bond direction and a *prioritized third atom* for planarity, then draws the centre line plus one inset parallel line (`valence_mode 1`), or two symmetric lines when that mode is off, with a triple doubling the offset. What stops it is that **chimol has no bond orders**: `bond_order` returns 1 for everything except a bond made by hand with the `bond` command, because bonds are inferred from distance and a distance carries no order. `set valence, on` would therefore leave every deposited structure looking exactly as it does -- the accepted-and-inert failure the settings table exists to prevent. Unblocking it is a *reader* change: mmCIF's `chem_comp_bond` carries orders for ligands, a PDB's `CONECT` does not, and perception from geometry is the third option.

* **Literature: one bibliography, one page, every citation a link** ([documentation browser](subsystems/documentation-browser.md)).

  A paper was written out wherever it was needed — sometimes with a DOI, usually without, in a different order each time, and never in a form a reader could click. Two pages citing the same work said it differently, and nothing could list what the documentation rests on. Now **`docs/references/bibliography.yaml` is the single source** for all 69 works, a page cites one with `` {cite}`key` ``, and a **Literature** section (in the help tree and in the published site) lists every entry. The role is expanded by the *same module* in both renderers — a Sphinx role in `docs/_ext/cite_role.py`, `api/bibliography.py` in the browser — so a reference reads and links identically in the application and on the website, and there is one place to correct it.

  **Each entry leads to the paper**: to its DOI where one is recorded, and otherwise to a literature search for the title. That asymmetry is deliberate — a reader who wants a paper wants a way to *get* it, and sending them to a guessed DOI is worse than sending them to a search, so a work whose identifier is not known simply does not get one invented. 65 of the 66 bullets in the pages' own reference lists were converted to keys automatically and the two that resisted were done by hand; a test fails on any citation key the bibliography does not define, and another fails when the generated page is stale.

  **Three defects the audit of the whole help surface turned up, all invisible until rendered.** A heading containing a formula or code produced a **broken id** — the placeholder token was substituted inside the `id="…"` attribute and the closing quote spilled into the page, so `## Where the reference $D$ comes from` displayed as `D-comes-from">Where the reference D comes from`. Root-relative image paths (`/guides/figures/x.png`, which is how Sphinx reads them) were handed to Qt as *filesystem* paths and silently missing. And a `{doc}` target naming an `.rst` page or a directory index resolved to nothing, which is why the guides' own pointer to the concepts was dead. Shipped documentation also still carried a fragment of leaked tool markup (`</content></invoke>`) at the end of a concept page.

  **Every plugin is in the catalogue now.** The generator walked `manifest.json` files only, so 13 plugins that declare themselves in code — including the FCS correlator and five TTTR tools — appeared in the menus and in the help tree while having no reference page at all. They are generated from the metadata the plugin loader actually reads, and their page says the manifest is missing rather than pretending otherwise.

  **Review tracking now covers what the browser serves**: `concepts`, `guides`, `getting_started`, `reference` and `references` join `manual`. That is deliberately uncomfortable — `0 reviewed, 79 AI-reviewed, 230 unreviewed` — because the 230 have had an automated audit (stubs, holes in sentences, dead links and cross-references, missing images, markup leaks, formulas rendered as images) but not a reading for correctness, and the tally is the worklist rather than a score.

* **`cell` draws the unit cell -- and drawing it showed that `symexp` had never worked** ([pymol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)).

  The box is not transcribed from anywhere: a cell is fully determined by its six parameters and `UnitCell.frac_to_real` already exists, so the twelve edges are that matrix applied to the corners of the unit cube. `cell [selection [, on|off|toggle]]`, per object because two structures in a scene can come from different crystals, with `cell_color` beside the three representation overrides.

  **What it exposed is the real find.** `symexp` builds the crystallographic mates around a molecule; every command reported success, the objects appeared in the panel, the atom coordinates were right -- and the picture was **one molecule**. Each object is drawn centred on its own centroid, so every mate was re-centred onto itself and landed at the render origin: six mates with six distinct centroids in Angstrom, all drawn at `(0, 0, 0)`, stacked on the original. `symexp` exists to show how molecules pack, so this removed the feature entirely while looking like it worked. `create`/`extract` had already solved it (`_reframe_to` moves the render arrays into the parent's frame and leaves the stored coordinates alone); the mates never got the call.

  **Why it went unnoticed is the lesson, and it is this file's recurring one.** The symmetry work was verified through the *operators* -- 7658 of them, closure modulo lattice translations, det ±1, one identity -- and through the mates' **coordinates**. Both were correct. Nothing looked at where they were **drawn**. A test that a transform is right is not a test that its result is visible in the right place, and it took giving the scene something with an absolute position, the cell box, for the two to disagree out loud. The guard compares the distances as drawn against the distances in Angstrom.

  Also recorded there: the `junk/pymol-open-source` checkout -- the tracker's stated authority on PyMOL behaviour -- was removed during this session, and `junk/clone.sh` restores it. 6 tests.

* **The first three appearance settings, which are one mechanism under three names** ([pymol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)).

  With the two-stores blocker cleared, the measured worklist starts: `stick_color`, `cartoon_color` and `surface_color`. PyMOL implements all three with the same line repeated in each representation -- `c != cColorDefault ? c : ai->color` (`RepCylBond.cpp`, `RepSurface.cpp`, `RepRibbon.cpp`) -- so there is one rule here too, read by each representation as it assembles its colours. The sentinel is stored as `None` rather than PyMOL's -1, because a negative number is not a colour and a config full of -1 says nothing to whoever reads it; `-1`, `default`, `none` and `atom` all clear an override.

  **Two things the implementation turned on.** The override must be read where the representation builds its colours, *not* folded into the shared per-residue array -- that array feeds the cartoon **and** the trace, so one fold would colour both. And the colour parser had to move: it lived in the command layer, which the renderer cannot call, so `colors.as_rgba` is the shared reader now (names, hex, sequences) while the command layer keeps the part that is session state, the colours defined with `set_color`.

  `ribbon_color` is **deliberately not registered**: chimol has no separate ribbon representation -- `show ribbon` already aliases the cartoon -- so the name would colour something other than what a PyMOL user means by it.

  8 tests, checking the three things that separate a setting that works from one that is merely registered: the override reaches the geometry it names, reaches **only** that one, and clearing it puts the atoms' colours back. They read the built scene rather than pixels, since shading is applied on top and an exact colour comparison would be a test of the ambient occlusion. Verified in a real window as a figure: sky-blue cartoon, orange ligand sticks, translucent pale-green surface over residues 1-40.

* **Inline formulas are text again, and the navigation icons are back** ([documentation browser](subsystems/documentation-browser.md)).

  **A picture in the middle of a sentence is the thing to avoid.** A rasterised inline formula sits at its own baseline, in its own font, at a size that stops matching the moment anything around it changes — and a tall one (a fraction, a sum with limits) shoves the line apart and floats above the words, which is what "the equations look horrible" was a photograph of: `x_i = a_i/\sum_j a_j` set as an image twice the height of the line it interrupted. Inline mathematics now converts to **HTML text** wherever it possibly can: slashed fractions that keep precedence (`(a+b)/c`, never `a+b/c`), big operators with their limits as ordinary sub- and superscripts, combining accents for `\hat`/`\bar`/`\vec`, script letters, upright function names, roots. Across `docs/` that is **102 rasterised inline formulas down to 5** — all matrices, genuinely two-dimensional, and those now carry `vertical-align: middle` so they at least sit on the line rather than hanging off it. Display mathematics is unchanged: it *should* be a picture, and it is a transparent one. A test holds the count.

  **The icons were removed for the wrong reason.** They had to leave the row's *text* — an emoji there makes Qt fall back to a colour font for the whole item and the fallback's metrics restyle the row — but that was an argument about where they live, not about whether they should exist. They are painted into a pixmap and set as the item's **icon** now: the sections have their glyphs back, the review badge rides in the same slot on a page row while authoring, and the label is still the application's own font.

* **The settings blocker is cleared: a key can change section now, and three settings stopped having two stores** ([pymol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)).

  The tracker's item 1a said *do this before registering anything else*, because a name registered against a store the renderer re-reads only at construction is accepted, echoed and **inert** -- which is what `surface_quality` turned out to be, four times over. It was three settings, not two.

  `depth_cue` / `fog` / `fog_start` are PyMOL's and are **global**: both renderers read them. They were registered under `ray.*` from when only the tracer honoured them, so the prefix said something untrue. Moving them needed the loader extension the tracker predicted -- `DISPLAY_CONFIG_MIGRATIONS` can only change a *value* -- so `DISPLAY_CONFIG_KEY_MOVES` sits beside it, and **its rule is the mirror image**, which is the part worth remembering: a value migration moves what the user did *not* choose (it still equals the old default), a key move carries across what they *did*, and drops the old key either way so the section it left keeps no stale twin. They are `depth_cue.enabled` / `.start` / `.intensity`; config version 8 -> 9. Six tests, including one that asserts every move's destination is a key the package actually ships -- a move to a key that is not there writes a value nothing reads, which is worse than not moving it.

  With 1a closed the appearance worklist (228 names PyMOL's own Python layer references) is unblocked, and the pattern every one of them must follow is `_fog_planes`: **read the configuration where the value is used**, never at construction.

* **Startup died in the dynamic loader because an IDE had source-rooted another environment** ([environment & build](workflows/build-and-env.md)).

  `<conda python> -m chisurf` failed at `import tttrlib` with `Library not loaded: @rpath/libhdf5.320.dylib`, which reads as the known two-environments-two-HDF5s build problem and was not it — both environments held a build they could load. The extension being loaded came from the **pixi** environment while the rpath resolving its libraries came from the **conda** interpreter, whose `lib/` has `libhdf5.310`. `@rpath` is resolved against the running executable's load commands, so an extension is only loadable by the interpreter it was installed for, and `sys.path` carries no notion of which environment an entry belongs to: the import succeeds and the *load* fails.

  **The mechanism is worth remembering because the culprit is not on the command line.** `.idea/chisurf.iml` had that `site-packages` marked as a **source root**, and an IDE prepends every source root to `PYTHONPATH` for all run configurations, whichever interpreter they select. Twelve such roots had accumulated — both pixi environments, a rattler build tree, and nine Python 3.10 benchmark virtualenvs, one pinning an *older* photon library. They are excluded now instead. Reproduced byte-for-byte with `PYTHONPATH=<pixi site-packages> <conda python> -c "import tttrlib"`, which is the cheap way to confirm this diagnosis rather than the build one.

  `chisurf.__init__` no longer depends on that file being right: `drop_foreign_environment_paths()` drops any `sys.path` entry that is the `site-packages` or **standard library** of an environment other than the running interpreter's (compared against `sys.prefix` *and* `sys.base_prefix`, so a virtualenv still reaches its system packages), before the first ChiSurf import — after one, the first compiled extension has already resolved against the wrong environment. A foreign standard library is the worse of the two, since it shadows the running interpreter's own modules. It warns with the entry, the interpreter and the likely cause; `CHISURF_ALLOW_FOREIGN_ENVIRONMENT_PATHS=1` opts out. 6 tests in `test/test_foreign_environment_paths.py` (layout recognition, both directions of the prefix check, the escape hatch, and a subprocess launch with a poisoned `PYTHONPATH`); the full GUI now reaches "Background startup complete" under that same `PYTHONPATH`, and the canonical pixi environment keeps its own paths untouched.

* **PRD-83: retire pyqtgraph — and the 3-D half nobody owned is closed** ([PRD-83](prds/prd-83.md), [PRD-64](prds/prd-64.md), [chiplot](subsystems/chiplot.md)).

  `pyqtgraph` is a declared dependency reached from **14 files**, one `.native` escape hatch with **12** entries, and **three subsystems that are not plotting at all**: `pyqtgraph.opengl` (chiplot's own 3-D volume view, and the exploration tool's UMAP plot), `pyqtgraph.parametertree` (a property sheet, whose in-tree comparison is AutoForm) and `pyqtgraph.dockarea`. PRD-64 owns the 2-D seam and describes a *backend swap*, which is the wrong frame for three of those four — which is how they stayed unowned. PRD-83 owns the end state instead: **is pyqtgraph still installed, and what is the last thing keeping it here?** Its definition of done ends at `pyqtgraph` leaving `pixi.toml`.

  **ChiMOL renders through PyOpenGL and imports nothing from pyqtgraph.** It had not rendered through pyqtgraph for a long time — `renderer/qtgl.py` is a `QOpenGLWidget` with its own shaders, matrices and picking — but the plugin's only allow-list entry was `renderer/backend.py`: 13 lines, `import pyqtgraph.opengl`, computing a `_HAVE_GL` flag whose **only** consumer was an import in `chimol/__init__.py` that does not even re-export it. The list said ChiMOL was unported when the unported thing was a file nobody used. (My first grep for importers used the wrong pattern and said *nothing* imported it; the test suite said otherwise, which is the argument for running it before believing a grep.)

  **The shim it left behind was not merely unnecessary, it was the bug.** `self.opts` mirrored `fov` and `center` under the comment *"Compatibility with picking helpers"*, beside a `cameraPosition()` returning a `QVector3D` — pyqtgraph's `GLViewWidget` camera API. `opts["center"]` was maintained by `_update_center_opt` from **seven** call sites and read by **nothing**, while the real value was recomputed on demand in `_build_matrices`; `opts["fov"]` was a second copy of `self._fov`. And the picking helper the shim existed for read that `QVector3D` straight into `numpy.asarray`, which raises — so **every click in the viewport raised**, silently. A compatibility layer nobody re-checks becomes a second store of a derived value, and here it broke its own only consumer. Shim, mirror and module are gone; the allow-list is 15 → **14**, struck rather than edited.



* **Clicking a residue in the viewport did not work, in four ways at once** ([pymol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)).

  The most-used thing in a molecular viewer, and nothing exercised it. (1) The picker projected atoms with a camera basis built from `view.cameraPosition()` and a `view.opts` dictionary -- **pyqtgraph's** `GLViewWidget` API, left behind when the renderer was replaced; the renderer kept an `opts` shim "for compatibility with picking helpers" whose `center` is a `QVector3D`, which the helper handed to `numpy.asarray`. Every click **raised**. (2) The raise was swallowed by `except Exception: pass`, so there was no message and no traceback. (3) The whole block was gated on `getattr(self, "_gl_enabled", False)` and **no code anywhere sets `_gl_enabled`** -- a dead attribute name in front of the feature. (4) A picked atom mapped to no residue: `set_coordinates`, which is what `apply_payload` (*"the single route from a file into the viewer"*) calls, cleared `_all_atom_res_ids` and never refilled it although `set_structure` fills it from the same field -- so for **RMF, mmCIF and every bead model** the pick succeeded and then had nothing to select.

  **The tests were green throughout, and that is the finding worth keeping.** `test_mouse_selection.py` stubbed the picking module, set `viewer._gl_enabled = True` *itself* -- supplying by hand the gate the product never sets -- and replaced `viewer.view` with a bare `object()`. Each substitution replaced something broken with something that was not. **A fixture is an assertion too**, and these asserted the broken environment into existence. The tests now send real `QMouseEvent`s through the real widget and read the selection out; the merge-logic tests that legitimately stub are kept below a divider that says which is which.

  **The projection lives on the renderer now** (`project_to_screen`), through the same matrices `paintGL` uses -- a picker that computes its own picks where the molecule is not. Two things it must respect and a from-scratch version keeps missing: the viewport is the **scene column**, not the widget, and it sits **below the sequence strip**.

  **The mouse block promised more than the mouse did**, all of it the same shape -- the *button* decided the gesture instead of the action the table resolves. The **middle button** was turned into a pan before the table was consulted, so `-Box`, `PkAt` and `Orig` were unreachable; `Ctrl L` is `Move` and rotated; a **ctrl-shift click** did nothing, because the press correctly claimed `Sele` for a rubber band and a band that is never dragged fell through a zero-size rectangle (each box action now degenerates to the same operation on the atom under the cursor); `Orig` was drawn and wired to nothing. And `mouseReleaseEvent` was **defined twice** -- Python keeps the last, so the one that ended the middle-button pan never ran and after a single middle-drag the molecule followed the cursor for the session. There was a comment saying so; a note that code is dead leaves the dead code there to be edited.

  19 tests, including one that walks **every cell of the block** and asserts the press starts the gesture the cell names. Verified in a real window: a shift-drag box takes 53 residues, highlighted in the 3-D view and in the sequence strip.

* **`silhouette` had two stores, so `set silhouette, on` could not exist** ([pymol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). The settings lived on the renderer's `PostProcess` object *and* in `_DISPLAY_CONFIG["silhouette"]`, read exactly once in `QtGLRenderer.__init__` -- so `lighting silhouette=on` moved the picture without touching the configuration, and the configuration was a start-up default no live change could reach. Registering the name against that store would have produced exactly the accepted-and-inert setting `surface_quality` turned out to be four times over. `PostProcess` reads the section through properties now: one store, read where it is used, so an already-constructed renderer sees a `set`. With that true the names are safe to register, and `silhouette`, `silhouette_thickness`, `depth_jump` and `silhouette_color` are.


* **"An agent read this page" is now a tracked state, and the whole manual is in it** ([documentation browser](subsystems/documentation-browser.md)).

  The sign-off ladder is `unreviewed → ai-reviewed → reviewed`. The middle rung exists because it is real: an agent can read a page end to end and correct what it can verify against the source code, but it cannot open the application, so it cannot tell whether a screenshot still matches the interface or whether a procedure still works. Collapsing that into *unreviewed* throws away the only signal that says which pages still need the **first** pass — and with 79 pages that was the difference between "nobody knows" and "one specific kind of check is missing".

  **Three properties keep the weaker level from being mistaken for the stronger one**, each with a test: an agent's sign-off does not clear the release gate (`review-check` still exits non-zero and `report.ok` stays human-only); an agent never overwrites a human's record, so a sweep over a directory cannot quietly erase what somebody actually checked; and either level goes stale the moment the page is edited, with the record remembering which level expired. `reviewer_kind` is stored explicitly rather than inferred from the reviewer's name, and registries written before the level existed read back as human sign-offs.

  Recorded from the GUI (*Authoring → 🤖 AI-reviewed*), over RPC, or in bulk with `csc help review-set docs/manual/*.rst --ai`. In the tree the state is a **row colour, not a badge character** — an emoji makes Qt fall back to a colour font for the whole item, so a badged manual was set in a different face from everything above it, exactly while somebody worked through it.

  **The pass itself covered all 79 pages**, and the second half turned up what the first had not: a JSON model file that is YAML and lives elsewhere (`fcs.model.json` → `chisurf/core/models/fcs/models.yaml`), with the wrong advice to overwrite it inside the installation rather than override it from the user folder; a simulated data set described with its slow species 1000× too fast, contradicting the page that generated it; a discrete-FRET page that claimed each donor-acceptor pair has its own rate and then that all of them share one; a sentence that stopped mid-clause; "(ii)" twice in a two-item list. `csc help review-list` now reports **0 reviewed, 79 AI-reviewed, 0 stale, 0 unreviewed** — the gate still fails, correctly, and it now says what kind of check is missing.

* **Data groups specified: a store becomes a tree, and the file becomes the serialisation of it** ([PRD-82](prds/prd-82.md), [columnar store](subsystems/columnar-store.md)).

  Written up as a requirements spec for the library to implement (its PRD-019, local to that checkout). The scope grew in the writing, and the growth is the point: the first draft was "let the HDF5 writer stop truncating", which is a file-format patch for a **container** that cannot express the shape either. A `DataStore` gains named child groups — each a full store with its own columns, row count, validity masks and selection — and an HDF5 group *is* a store group, so writing a file is writing the tree and a store with no children serialises exactly as it does today.

  Why several tables and not one: the row counts differ. Per-pixel imaging is a `results` table of one row per pixel plus a one-row `meta` back-reference to the photon file; a burst export is a per-photon table plus a per-burst summary. Each is several tables that are meaningless apart, and today the caller either invents a file-naming convention and loses the association or keeps the data-frame HDF5 layer for its multi-key files — which is exactly what still ties those writers to the native dependency this library could replace.

  **The reader is already there**, measured rather than assumed: a root table with a `/meta` sub-group beside it — built with a third-party HDF5 writer, since the library cannot yet produce it — reads back correctly, sub-group ignored, dtypes kept. So the file half is write-side plus one strictness change (a read of an absent group must throw, not answer with an empty store that is indistinguishable from a zero-row table).

  Two requirements carry scars. **Reference stability for group handles is a stated requirement**, not an implementation detail, because the equivalent bug already shipped here once — columns in a `std::vector`, a reference handed out, the next `add()` reallocating it into freed memory that reads as an empty column. And **column order is link-creation order and is easy to lose**: the same datasets written without creation-order tracking read back alphabetically, so the property must be set on every group the new paths create, including the temporary one that gets moved into place.

* **The Lifetime editor is the JSON one now, and a migration has to prove it lost nothing** ([PRD-38](prds/prd-38.md), [GUI & AutoForm](subsystems/gui-autoform.md), [testing](workflows/testing.md)).

  The fitting-model editors were asked to be screened: which are modern, which are ancient. PRD-38 already owned the work and its frontmatter promised a status table — but the file had none, so the whole per-model backlog was one prose sentence, and the PRD claimed a Lifetime flip that had been **reverted without being recorded**. A plan built on it would have been a plan against fiction. PRD-38 now carries the per-model **STATUS TABLE**, tiered by *what blocks each model*: portable today, blocked on getting compute out of the GUI file (7 models, ~5.6k LOC), needs a new section, or dead. The re-derivation commands are in the table, because the trap is counting files instead of registrations — a `view.json` can exist for a model nobody can open, and a legacy widget file can be 76% dead while still exporting one live class, which is exactly the shape of `pda2c/widgets.py`.

  **"Prefer AutoForm tables" turned out to be universal practice nobody had written down**: all 57 parameter-group sections in the tree are `parameter_group_table` and *none* is the verbose form. Now stated repo-wide with the criterion for the exception, and `Model.view_spec()`'s auto-derive fallback emits the table form too — it had been handing unauthored models the one layout no authored spec chose.

  The Lifetime flip landed for real, and the **before/after screenshot rule** is why it is trustworthy. Two of the three parity gaps PRD-38 listed were already closed (rotation add/remove exists; FWHM is drawn by the IRF widget). The comparison then found a fourth nobody had listed — the `#PhB`/`#PhF` photon counts, computed properties rather than parameters, so the parameter table correctly skipped them and they had silently disappeared. It also surfaced a latent bug: `unload_background_curve` read `model.nuisance` where the group is `generic`, so the action raised into a bare `except: pass` and had **never worked**. One gap remains: the anisotropy r(t) diagnostics panel, which needs a new section.

  *The rule that makes this repeatable:* capture the legacy widget **before** touching it — afterwards the baseline is unrecoverable — and compare **control inventory, not pixels**, because a port deliberately changes layout and any SSIM gate is either always red or worthless. Two traps, both hit here: a parameter name that moved into a table cell reads as "lost" to `findChildren(QLabel)`, and renames (`r[MHz]`→`rep`, `Linearize`→`DNL`) read as losses too. `test/gui/migration_parity.py` handles both.

  **A round of layout work on the generated editors**, each item of which turned out
  to be a framework gap rather than a per-model tweak. The add/remove buttons were
  stretching to half the panel width each in saturated green and red above *every*
  component table — now sized to their text with a trailing spacer and muted. A set
  of parameters belonging to the *model* rather than a nested group could not be a
  table at all, so chain and maximum-entropy models were columns of standalone rows;
  `parameter_group_table` gained `parameters_source` and `row_width` with row/slot
  labels, which also lets a group that is really a **matrix** show itself as one —
  PDDEM's ten parameters are five named quantities × fluorophore A/B and now read as
  a 5×2 table. *Row labels live in a table cell, so unlike column headers they are
  not rich text: `&alpha;` rendered literally until it became `α`.*

  **Tables now shed columns by priority as they narrow, and the `bounds` toggle is
  gone** — the width check made it redundant, so bounds are always wanted and only
  space hides them (the `bounds_toggle` spec field went with it, out of 11 specs).
  Bounds go first, then the error, then the fixed flag — all three reachable in the
  parameter popup — and name/value are never dropped. The third tier exists because
  two were not enough: a table packing four parameters per row still overflowed a
  dock once bounds and errors were gone, which is the multi-column case that looked
  fixed and was not.

  *The measurement is the interesting part.* Summing column size hints was wrong in
  both directions — a **stretch** column is given more than its hint, so wide tables
  looked overfull and dropped everything; every section is floored at a minimum and
  the paired table's value columns switch between stretching and hugging, so narrow
  tables measured as fitting and then scrolled anyway. It now **applies a candidate
  set and asks the header how wide it came out**. In the paired table the column
  choice and the value-column policy depend on each other, so it settles, chooses,
  settles again. Separately: a table inside a *collapsed* panel is never resized
  while hidden, so expanding one used to reveal every column and a sideways
  scrollbar — decided on show as well as resize now.

  Three of my own guards were worth less than they looked: one asserted the
  multi-slot case against a model with no table wider than two slots and so checked
  nothing; one measured overflow by summing hints the widget deliberately ignores;
  one demanded no scrolling where scrolling is the documented choice over eliding a
  number. All rewritten to assert the visible outcome. A headless test of any of
  this must `show()` the editor and use `setFixedWidth` — `resize()` alone is refused
  below a layout's minimum, so the first harness I wrote narrowed nothing and proved
  nothing.

  **The parse family went next, and the section it was supposed to need did not
  exist for a reason.** PRD-38 had it filed as the one genuine tier-C item — a
  bespoke equation-catalogue widget. But the catalogue was only *bespoke* because it
  lived in the Qt widget: `ParseModel._models` was a dict nothing ever filled, so
  picking an equation was not something a script or a view spec could do. Moving the
  catalogue into core made the editor ordinary vocabulary — a `choice` over
  `catalogue_names`, a `value` on `func`, an `info` for the description, a parameter
  table — and retired four registered models (TCSPC decay, FCS, PCF, stopped flow)
  with **no new section at all**.

  Two of those four were not merely un-ported but **unopenable**. The stopped-flow
  parse model passed a `str` where a `pathlib.Path` was expected *and* pointed at a
  catalogue file that is not in the tree, so it raised `AttributeError` on
  construction; it now has a core model and the catalogue it never had. And
  `EtModelFreeWidget` — still in the menu — is **abstract**, missing `update_model`,
  so choosing it can only fail. Nothing constructs these, which is why nothing
  noticed.

  Two framework fixes worth more than the ports: `info`'s `source` and the new
  `parameters_source` demanded a *method*, so naming a property or a list rendered
  an empty box or dropped a whole table with at most a warning — a trap already
  recorded once as a gotcha, now fixed at the resolver. And catalogue initial values
  are **seeded when the equation is parsed** rather than applied after selection,
  because any re-parse rebuilds the parameter objects and building the editor
  triggers one: `Mode` opened at 1 where the catalogue says 20.

  *Also worth knowing:* the shared test fixture built its data on an axis starting at
  zero, which makes a `log(x)` equation legitimately non-finite — a correct model
  looked broken until the axis became strictly positive, which is what a time or lag
  axis is anyway.

  **Global fit followed** — `global_parameter_table` was built, tested and used by
  *nothing*, and is now this editor's parameter view, so it shows every parameter of
  every fit plus the registered out-of-fit groups instead of one hand-rolled table.
  `globalfit.ui` is gone. One contract worth knowing: `button_row`'s `action` is a
  **zero-arg model method**, not a dispatcher action, and the existing `model.*`
  actions all need arguments — so the selection state moved onto the model
  (`selected_local_fit`, `selected_candidate_fit`, `new_global_parameter_name`) and
  the buttons call zero-arg methods over it. That is what let the list, the picker
  and the buttons all be generic sections with no widget state.

  **The remaining `.ui` files are now mapped one by one** rather than counted. Two
  (`tcspc_convolve.ui`, `tcspcCorrections.ui`) are already dead: their widgets are
  reachable only from `LifetimeModelWidgetBase`, which no registered model uses. But
  deleting that ~2.5k-LOC layer has to happen in one change with two conditions, or
  it is a regression — `anisotropy.py` holds the r(t) diagnostics panel that is the
  single un-ported control of every FRET/Lifetime editor, so removing it destroys the
  reference before its replacement exists; and a contract test AST-inspects
  `ConvolveWidget`. The other four each block on exactly one thing: an `EtModelFree`
  extraction, an `expression` field (validity badge + LaTeX), a catalogue API for
  Python `code:` rather than equations, and a reaction-scheme section.

  **Then the hand-written TCSPC widget layer was deleted outright.**
  `gui/widgets/models/tcspc/` went from ~5k LOC to an alias module plus the two
  κ²/Förster helpers the `kappa2_controls` section calls: once every TCSPC model was
  data-described, `LifetimeModelWidgetBase` and the convolve/corrections/generic/
  anisotropy/gaussian/discrete-distance widgets were reachable only from each other.
  Three `.ui` files went with them, and `parameter_transform.ui` with the parameter
  transform — whose catalogue holds a Python `code:` block rather than an
  `equation:`, which turned out to be **two class attributes** on a shared catalogue
  mixin rather than a second implementation. **Two `.ui` files remain under
  `models/`**, each with one named blocker.

  Three registered models turned out to be **abstract** — `EtModelFreeWidget`,
  `ReactionWidget`, and the old stopped-flow parse model — so each could only raise
  when chosen from the menu. Nothing constructs a model widget in the test suite,
  which is why none of it surfaced. The ET fit is now deprecated by decision rather
  than ported.

  Two costs of the deletion, both paid rather than deferred: a contract test that
  AST-inspected `ConvolveWidget` for button handlers is gone (its subject is gone;
  the macro/action contracts that outlive it are kept), and the **r(t) diagnostics
  panel** — still the one un-ported control of the FRET/Lifetime editors — now
  exists only in git history, with the recovery SHA written down in known-issues.
  A third caller was also found appending onto a component list the model now seeds,
  the same defect already fixed twice; the fix is to *define* the ensemble rather
  than append onto whatever the constructor left.

  **The r(t) diagnostics panel is back, as a section.** Deleting it with the widget
  layer was a mistake — it was the one un-ported control of every FRET/Lifetime
  editor and its only implementation. It is now `anisotropy_diagnostics`, declared in
  all ten specs that have an Anisotropy panel, with every control the dialog had. The
  port changed three things rather than copying them: the window is **modeless**
  (`exec_()` blocks the event loop, and offscreen it blocks with nobody able to close
  it — which is why the old panel could never be screenshotted); the anisotropy
  algebra moved into core as `Anisotropy.rt_from_channels`, so the numbers the plot
  draws can be asserted without a display; and the CSV export pads rather than
  interpolating, because data and model have independent time axes and resampling
  would write numbers the fit never computed.

  **Two of the six core extractions landed** (FIDA and multi-component PCH), and
  they identified the pattern behind all of them: a computed output written through
  `get_fitting_client()` from inside `update_model`, wrapped in a bare `except`. It
  does nothing whenever that client is absent — headless, or before the editor has
  registered the fit — so PCH's "add component" button had never worked outside a
  live GUI. A direct parameter write is the fix. The PCH histogram maths moved to
  core with the model: four numpy functions had been living in a Qt module, so the
  distribution could not be computed or checked against a reference without
  importing the GUI.

  *Two attempts to script the third extraction produced a broken module and were
  thrown away.* Those fitting-client blocks are `try:` bodies that also contain the
  statements computing the value being published, and one sits inside a `for` loop —
  so removing the block removes the computation, and filtering "plumbing" lines by
  pattern breaks the indentation. It is a by-hand job; the note is in PRD-38 so the
  next attempt does not start the same way.

  Also: `LifetimeModel.name` was `"Lifetime "` with a trailing space, which stopped being cosmetic the moment the primary entry is matched *by name* against an `==` comparison; name fixed and the match made whitespace-tolerant. `"Lifetime (new)"` had become a de-facto API string in 13 test files. 45 tests green; the 5 stray `.ui` files inside the Qt-free `core/models/**` are gone.

* **`build-tttrlib` now leaves every environment able to import what it built** ([build and env](workflows/build-and-env.md), [known issues](references/known-issues.md)).

  One build served two environments by symlink, which works only while both agree on the native libraries it links — and they do not: the solved environment takes HDF5 2.1, the sibling conda environment carries 1.14, so the shared extension is unloadable there (`Library not loaded: @rpath/libhdf5.320.dylib`). The task **reported success anyway**, because it verified only the environment it installed *into*; the sibling broke silently and surfaced later as a suite that could not collect.

  A link that cannot be loaded is now repaired instead of reported: `link_build()` checks each target actually imports, and where it does not — mismatched native libraries, or a different CPython ABI — `_build_into()` builds that environment its own extension against its own prefix and installs it as **real files rather than symlinks**, codesigned, so the next shared build cannot silently point it back at something unloadable. `main()` returns non-zero if any target still cannot import, so this can no longer pass as a green build.

  Verified by reproducing the exact broken state — the unloadable symlink restored by hand — and running the link step: it detected it, rebuilt for the sibling, and verified the import. The `add()`-lifetime fix is live in both environments. 106 tests green.

* **The manual's prose, and three things a reader noticed immediately** ([documentation browser](subsystems/documentation-browser.md)).

  **The manual was a docx conversion, and the conversion had eaten things.** A page whose whole body was the word "Missing"; a title slide as the *Introduction*; three worked-example pages whose sentences had holes where an inline equation used to be ("the donor fluorescence in the absence of an acceptor, , can be plotted"); citations that had become "()"; menu paths whose arrow was gone ("File"  "Add dataset"); superscripts flattened into the number beside them (`6.022*1023 mol-1`); and "Open Chisurf2016". None of it fails a build, and a reader meets all of it. Every instance is fixed, and the classes are now guarded — `test_manual_snippets.py` fails on a stub page, on a hole in a sentence, and on an empty citation.

  **Code in a manual has to be code that runs.** Two snippets were teaching the wrong thing: `chisurf.parameter.Parameter` (the module is `chisurf.core.parameter`) and `sample_fit(fit, filename="…er4")`, whose second argument became a **directory** when sampling grew diagnostics — the shown call would create a directory named after a file. Both are corrected, the sampling page now documents all six samplers rather than the one it had, and a test resolves every `chisurf.…` name in every snippet and checks `sample_fit`'s first two parameters against its real signature. The FRET-line pages set their R_DA axis with `np.logspace(start=np.log(1), stop=np.log(500))` — that is an axis running to 1.6 × 10⁶ Å, three orders of magnitude past the intended 500.

  **Pages rewritten from the source rather than tidied:** PDDEM (parameters read off the model class, Kalinin & Johansson cited), the worm-like chain (contour and persistence length, the Becker/Rosa/Everaers distribution, and what κ = l_p/l means), the F-Calculator, the lifetime model's three convolution modes, and `parameter_optimization`, whose settings section had dissolved into a code block and appeared twice. The FRET-line page's definitions of τ_x and τ_f were the wrong way round, and its "mathematical basis" gave a closed form that holds only for a single-exponential donor — the implementation builds the full lifetime spectrum, which is exactly what makes the line correct for the multi-exponential donors real dyes are.

  **Three defects a reader found in five minutes, all invisible to tests.** The navigation was set in a different face from the rest of the application — an emoji in a tree row makes Qt fall back to a colour font for that whole row, with different metrics; the icons are gone. There was no way to change the text size — Ctrl+± now re-renders the page at a new point size (a widget zoom would move the body text and leave every heading, table and formula behind) and re-typesets the formulas with it. And the manual's equations were unreadable: docutils emits MathML by default, which Qt cannot lay out, so it drew the leaf text of every node — `\tau_x` as "τ x", a fraction as numerator beside denominator. The writer now emits delimited LaTeX for our own typesetter, `\underbrace{X}_{label}` puts the label *under* the term instead of turning it into a subscript, and the glyphs are a sans maths font so a symbol looks the same in a sentence as in a displayed equation.

  Opening the window costs 0.6 s rather than 2.8: `Path.relative_to` in a per-file loop was 2.5 s of it, every page was read twice, and the review badges were fetched through a call that rediscovers every document in the project.

* **The environment is fixed, and trying stage 2 found what actually blocks it** ([PRD-82](prds/prd-82.md), [build and env](workflows/build-and-env.md), [known issues](references/known-issues.md)).

  **Both environments now carry the column-lifetime fix**, and the re-solve made the gap it was hiding measurable rather than predicted: a freshly solved environment has **no `pytables`**, so `to_hdf` raises there and **all seven** pandas HDF5 call sites are dead — not five, as the PRD had it; the burst-selection writer and the photon-filter wizard were missed. Developer environments work only because they still carry the package.

  **Three library gaps block stage 2, and two were found by attempting it.** A text column still inflates the file. The legacy read is *worse than "unsupported"*: handed a pandas-written file, `read_hdf5`, `read_hdf5_table` and `read_hdf5_table_columns` return an **empty store and an empty column tuple** while `isHDF5File` says `True` — so a migrated reader would open every existing user file blank and report success. The companion viewer already guards this correctly (`if len(columns) < 1: return None`), and that guard is the template until it is fixed in the library. And a **file cannot hold two groups**: the writer opens with `H5F_ACC_TRUNC`, so writing `meta` after `results` destroys `results` — verified, and it blocks the imaging format outright, which is exactly that shape.

  **A data-loss bug found on the way, fixed and pinned.** `add_maps_to_hdf5` rewrites the per-pixel table, so it first reads what is there — and turned *any* read failure into "there was no table", silently rewriting with only the new maps and reporting success. Demonstrated: running N&B over an imaging file in the columnar layout destroyed its lifetime map and returned `['N']`. "There is no file" and "I cannot read the file" are different answers, and conflating them costs an analysis. It now reads both layouts and **raises** on a file it cannot read; three tests cover the columnar merge, the unreadable file and the absent one.

  **Two build traps, both of which report success.** `pixi run build-tttrlib` could not configure on macOS at all because `hdf5` was declared for two platforms out of four — now in the common dependencies and in `_BUILD_ONLY` in the dependency guard, since it is a build dependency and not part of the released runtime. And the built library is shared between two environments **that disagree about HDF5** (2.1 against 1.14): the build verifies only the environment it installed into, so the symlinked sibling breaks silently and shows up as a suite that cannot import. The sibling now has its own build; re-running the task undoes that, and the durable fix — pin one HDF5, or verify the link target loads — is recorded rather than done.

* **The columnar store's memory-safety fix, verified — and the broken macOS build that was hiding it** ([columnar store](subsystems/columnar-store.md), [build and env](workflows/build-and-env.md), [known issues](references/known-issues.md), [PRD-82](prds/prd-82.md)).

  **The append case is fixed, and it is measured rather than assumed.** The library now holds its columns in a container whose references survive an append, so a `Column` held across fifty `add()` calls keeps its name, its data and its write-through, where the shipped build answers `''` and `[]`. Verified by building the library into a **scratch prefix** and running the suites under that `PYTHONPATH` — which touches neither environment, and matters because the lock file carries another session's uncommitted work.

  **Two things that survived the fix.** *Removal* still invalidates, and unevenly — a vector erase at index 2 leaves index 0 readable, a deque erase does not — so whether a given proxy is still good is not a contract in either build. And **the fix is in no built environment here**: the shipped binary is still the old one. So `column_at()` and the never-cache rule stay on both counts, and the test now asserts the *positive* invariant (`column_at` answers with live data across an append and a removal) rather than pinning a bug whose presence depends on the build. Both suites pass against the shipped build **and** the fixed one — 75 tests, twice.

  **Why the fix had not reached a binary: `hdf5` was declared for two platforms out of four.** It is a build dependency of the photon library, whose CMake requires it unconditionally, and it used to arrive by accident as a transitive dependency of the HDF5 table package. Dropping that package took it out of the macOS environment, and `build-tttrlib` has been unable to configure there ever since — "Could NOT find HDF5". Being declared for `win-64`/`linux-64` only is what made it read as platform-specific rather than as the missing dependency it is. Now in the common `[dependencies]`, and in `_BUILD_ONLY` in the declared-dependency guard, because it is not part of the released runtime.

  **Two traps worth naming, because both read as success.** `pixi run build-tttrlib | tail` reports the exit status of `tail` — a failed build looks green, and I read it that way once. And a failed build is not fatal to anything visible: the previously built library stays installed and importable, so a C++ change appears rebuilt when it is not. The only honest check is to assert the new behaviour from Python.

* **A frame carries more than coordinates: chimol plays a simulation, not just a trajectory** ([pymol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md), [chimol spec](specs/chimol.md)).

  **The use that forced it:** open a growing biofilm from the agent-simulation framework beside ChiSurf. An MD trajectory moves the same atoms for the whole file; a colony does not — cells appear, grow, and change what they are doing where they stand. RMF has always stored a **radius and a colour per frame**, and chimol read neither: radii were taken once *after* the frame loop, so they came from whichever frame the walk left current, and `ColoredConstFactory` was built in the loader and **never asked**, so a file stating its own colours was drawn in the viewer's defaults. Both are read per frame now and collapsed to one array when they do not vary, so a static model grows no time axis.

  **A radius of zero is how "does not exist yet" is said**, because an RMF's node set is fixed for the file. That needed a *third* visibility mask (`absent_mask`) rather than a reuse of `hidden_mask` — one mask for both questions means stepping the movie silently un-hides what the hierarchy panel switched off, the identical failure `representation_mask` was split out to avoid. All three compose in `visible_row_mask`. Passing zero through as a radius was not an option either: the renderers substitute a default for a non-positive one, so every unborn cell would have been drawn at full size from frame one.

  **The load was 19.7 s and is 2.16 s, and the reason generalises.** `numpy` converting a SWIG `RMF.Vector3` falls back to the **iteration protocol** — 20 us against 1.4 us for three plain subscripts. Over 60 frames x 2600 beads that was 17 s of the 19.7; the profile named `Vector3___getitem__` with 624 000 calls. The same spelling sat in the coordinate fallback path and went with it. A second one-liner: `np.array_equal(frames, frames[:1])` **does not broadcast** — it compares shapes first — so a series that never changes read as one that always does, and every static file grew a full time axis.

  **`IMP.rmf` cannot write what RMF can store.** `save_frame` snapshots `IMP.display.Colored` when the hierarchy is added, so every frame returns the colour the model started with. The simulator had built an elaborate workaround for that — one particle per cell **per observed state**, with the unused ones parked at (-100, -100, -100) — and the states it enumerated were always a set of one, because a cell's state was read from its own coordinates and a cell never moves once it is born. Writing through RMF directly gives per-frame colour and radius, so the workaround is gone: one node per cell.

  **The model had to change for the picture to mean anything.** State is now a property of the **neighbourhood** — depth below the *local* top of the film — so a cell's colour changes because the colony grew over it, which is what burial is. And growth is **surface-limited**: a placement that would put a daughter inside a neighbour *fails*, and a cell whose placements all fail leaves the dividing set. That one rule is the difference between a film and a smear — without it the colony packed 2600 cells (1812 um^3) into 1638 um^3 of film and never rose above 6.4 um over a 60 um plate; with it, 17.4 um and four visible strata. Two supporting fixes: hard-coded 4 um wall margins made a small domain impossible, and **seeding ignored the contact distance** the divisions enforced, so a run's closest pair of cells was reliably two seeds, 0.37 um apart. Found by the test, not by looking.

  **`bg_color` and `ray` were two stores for one setting** — the command writes to the renderer, the tracer read the startup config — so `bg_color white; ray` gave a white viewport and a black picture, in every figure ever traced. Fixed while making the guide figure. Trap: the renderer keeps **RGBA** and the tracer's parser accepted only a three-long sequence, so the live value fell through to the black fallback and the fix looked inert.

  **The camera was following the frame, and only a growing structure showed it.** `_select_state_frame` recomputed the object's centre and radius from the frame on show, so the camera chased the current frame's centroid -- the scene centre swung 0 -> -21 -> +52 scene units over the biofilm's run and the substratum slid about beneath a film that was supposed to be growing off it. On a molecule the extent barely changes and it reads as a gentle wander, which is why it survived; it was also hiding half of what the trajectory demo teaches, since following the centroid removes exactly the translational drift `intra_fit` is there to remove. Not deleted, because for a molecule wandering across a box that behaviour is the useful one: it is `movie_recenter` (`camera.recenter_on_frame`), on by default, read from the config **where it is used** so a live `set` reaches an open viewer and there is no second store to leave stale. `set` is global as it is in PyMOL, so each demo that cares now states the value it wants. The first version of the test passed **vacuously** -- the centre is computed over all rows, not the visible ones, so a fixture whose particles never move cannot exercise re-centring at all; it needed a drift term.

  **Shipped:** `Demo > Biofilm growth`, whose material is **generated on first use** (~3 s) and cached rather than checked in, so the demo is a result and not a picture of one; a concept page ([biofilm growth](../docs/concepts/biofilm_growth.md)) stating what the model does *not* do — no solute field, no mechanical relaxation, no detachment, thresholds chosen for visibility rather than measured; and the guide section on reading a per-frame radius and colour. Tests: 7 new in chimol (`test_rmf_frame_appearance.py`), 7 in the simulator (`tests/swarm/test_visual_runner.py`), one guardrail on the traced background; 31 demo tests, 70 RMF/bead/animation/session tests green.


* **The help a user actually reads: structure, rendering and search** ([documentation browser](subsystems/documentation-browser.md), [help buttons and guided tours](subsystems/gui-help-and-guides.md)).

  **The tree was a directory listing and is now the documentation's own table of contents.** Four buckets, each a flat alphabetical run of file names: the user manual arrived as 79 sibling rows sorted by filename, so *Calculations*, *Calculations* and *Calculation of confocal volume* sat together while the chapter each belonged to appeared nowhere, and the "Core" bucket offered a build script's README next to the changelog. `api/toc.py` reads the `toctree` blocks the published HTML is built from, so order, grouping and titles are the author's and one fix serves both surfaces. A `.. rubric::`, a `##` heading or a `:caption:` above a toctree names the group under it — nothing in the code enumerates *Fundamentals* or *Worked example — calibrating an FCS setup*. The manual's chapters therefore live in `docs/manual/index.rst`, and `convert_manual.py` now writes `index.generated.rst` **beside** it instead of over it, because that structure exists nowhere in the source document. The 59 guides were one `:glob:` run and are eight themed groups. Developer documentation and the review sign-off moved behind an *Authoring* toggle: a release gate is a maintainer's tool and was taking a third of the toolbar.

  **The pages that carry the most information rendered the worst.** Every concept page opened on its own `(concept-fret)=` anchor; its formulas read `\frac{1}{\tau_D}`; its admonitions read `:::{note}`; its cross-references read ``{ref}`concept-x``. All four are now rendered, and two tests hold it over the whole shipped tree — **every formula in `docs/` typesets**, and **no page leaks markup**. Inline mathematics is converted to HTML text (`τ<sub>D</sub>`) rather than rasterised, because an image sits on its own baseline in its own font; only two-dimensional constructs become pictures, drawn on a *transparent* figure since `math_to_image` bakes in a white background — a bright card behind every equation on a dark theme. Pages take the running palette, the text column is bounded, and images are scaled.

  **Three failure modes worth remembering.** An unknown directive is dropped *silently*: bare docutils parses at a report level where `.. seealso::` — which is how the manual points at the concept pages — produced nothing at all, so those links were not broken but invisible. Code and directive fences are the same syntax, so masking inline code first let the closing back-ticks of a ` ```{figure} ` block pair with the opening ones as one enormous code span, rendering a whole figure directive as pink monospace. And filtering a tree by the raw query string empties it — "anisotropy g-factor" appears verbatim in no row — so the tree is filtered by the *result set* of the search instead.

  **Cross-reference resolution moved into the Qt-free API** (`api/xref.py`), because the manual's reStructuredText renderer needs the same answers and cannot import a widget module. Both dialects now resolve, and a reference with no caption reads as the **title of the page it leads to** rather than as `concept-fcs-correlation`. A dead reference degrades to its own words, never to markup. 188 tests assert that every concept points at a guide, every guide at a concept, and every link resolves; `sphinx -b html` is warning-free.

  **matplotlib's mathtext is a subset of LaTeX** — 153 of 1965 formulas in `docs/` would not parse. They are rewritten first (`\boldsymbol`, `\mathsf`, `\tfrac`, `\le`, `\lVert`, `\underbrace`, brace-less `\frac12`, and newlines, which are a parse error rather than whitespace). Mapping `\big(`/`\big)` onto `\left`/`\right` *creates* unbalanced input; the modifier is dropped instead.

  **Still open:** the manual's *prose* is a machine-drafted docx conversion — 79 pages, none human-reviewed, several describing an older interface. The structure around it is now right, and `docs/manual/fit_of_a_fcs_curve.rst` shows what fixing one page looks like.

* **New rule: shipped source never names a PRD** ([change tracking](workflows/change-tracking.md)).

  A PRD is a planning artifact — it has a lifecycle, it gets superseded, and its number means nothing to someone reading the file, who cannot follow it from where they are. Point at the OKF **concept** that owns the area instead, or drop the reference, which is usually right. Scope is `chisurf/` (Python, `view.json`, YAML, shipped markdown); `okf/` is where PRDs live and `test/` documents process. Enforced by `test/test_prd_mentions.py` against `test/prd_mention_allowlist.txt` — **148 files, 243 mentions** grandfathered in, a *shrinking* list on the pyqtgraph-seam pattern, never somewhere to add yourself. A file you touch is a file you clean.

* **The first table on the columnar store** ([PRD-82](prds/prd-82.md), [columnar store](subsystems/columnar-store.md), [chitable](subsystems/gui-tables.md)).

  **Stage 1 landed.** `chisurf/core/datastore.py` is the Qt-free seam (`store_from_dataframe`, `dataframe_from_store`, `store_from_arrays`, `column_at`, `column_values`, `set_cell`, `clear_cell`) and `DataStoreSource` is chitable's fourth adapter. The conversions live in core, not in the widget, so that the GUI does not become the seam for stages 2–4. **75 tests green** (`test/test_datastore_seam.py`, `test/gui/test_chitable.py`): the filter, sort, colour-range and filtered-edit tests are parametrised over both sources, and one test walks every cell of both and asserts equality.

  **What the store does that a frame cannot**, each with a test: a `float32` column stays `float32` through a cell edit instead of being widened; blanking an integer cell sets the column's **validity mask** rather than writing a sentinel, so the column keeps its dtype *and* the difference between "zero" and "not measured"; and a text column edits as a drop-down of its own dictionary — while the dictionary is small (`MAX_CHOICE_LABELS = 64`), because a combo box of ten thousand burst ids is not an editor. The reverse conversion is **lossy in one documented direction**: a masked entry becomes `NaN` and widens an integer column, because a frame has nowhere else to put it.

  **A memory-safety bug in the library, found by writing the adapter the obvious way.** A `Column` from `add()` or `store[i]` is a reference into a `std::vector<Column>`; the next `add()` reallocates and the held proxy reads **freed memory** — reporting an empty name and an empty array rather than raising. The symptom is not a crash but a table that silently goes blank, which no assertion catches. The seam never caches a proxy, and a test pins the library behaviour so that it **fails once the library is fixed** — the signal to drop the workaround. The one-line root-cause fix (a stable-reference container) was *not* applied: another instance holds 308 uncommitted lines in that same header, so it could be written but not verified, and a break would be indistinguishable from mine. Recorded with the reproducer in [known issues](references/known-issues.md).

  **Two predictions the implementation corrected.** The PRD listed a single-cell text write as a blocking library gap (**T8**); it is not — it is expressible over `dictionary()`/`set_dictionary()`/`codes()`, which is what `set_cell` does. And two smaller gaps were found instead: a boolean column has no zero-copy view (it decodes through a per-row Python loop, so a write through the array it returns is silently lost) and `mask_numpy()` returns a copy. Stage 2 is still blocked on **T1** exactly as predicted — a text column written to HDF5 with its labels materialised makes the file *larger* than the pandas one it would replace.

* **A parameter is addressed by its own fit, not by its group.** `FitGroup.model` is the **selected** member's model, so a group uid addresses whichever member happens to be selected. `_parameter_context` reports the *group* uid as `fit_uid`, and `_rpc_address` was sending that — so a name-plus-fit write for a parameter of any *other* member silently landed on the selected member and returned `ok: True` (reproduced: editing member[1]'s `dt` wrote member[0]'s). The recorded provenance `fit_uid` (group) is unchanged — `history/replay.py` reads it. So a non-uniform axis is written to a `<name>.times.npy` sidecar and read back in preference to the header. `read_time_axis` is the single place that decision lives, so a reader and a test cannot disagree about it — which they did, twice, before it was centralised.

## 2026-08-05

* **ChiSurf decodes XTC itself, 1.8–2.2× faster than the reference C** ([PRD-80](prds/prd-80.md)). Second format after DCD, ported from GROMACS' `xdrfile` (BSD-2, again from the C rather than the LGPL wrapper). Unlike DCD this is a genuine decode — coordinates quantised to a stated precision, stored as integers relative to a per-frame bounding box, bit-packed — so the bit-level routines are numba kernels; there is no vectorised way to walk a bit stream.
  **The speed comes from parallelising across frames, not from the kernel.** Unpacking one frame is strictly serial, but each frame is a self-contained compressed block whose bit stream never crosses a frame boundary, so the frames are embarrassingly parallel. Medians of 5 on 5235 atoms: 50 frames **6.5 ms vs 12.4 ms**, 200 frames **26.2 vs 47.3**, 464 frames **61.4 vs 133.5**. Bit-exact against the reference on every branch — 1, 4, 9 (uncompressed), 10, 100, 5235 atoms.
  **Three silent traps, each of which cost a debugging cycle.** (1) `run` **persists** across atoms: when the flag bit is 0 the reference does not reset the run length, because a second water molecule of the same length should cost that one bit. Resetting it — the obvious-looking thing — decodes the first molecule and then walks off the stream. (2) The **≤9-atom branch has a different frame layout**: the coordinates sit behind the atom-count field that only the compressed branch otherwise reads, so a walker that misses it desynchronises four bytes in and reports "not an XTC file" at the *second* frame. (3) `lastbyte` is a **32-bit unsigned** in C and its shift discards the high bits; letting it grow in 64-bit changes what the next shift reads.
  **A lesson about oracles for lossy formats.** The first fixture stored the coordinates handed *to* the writer, and the test failed by 0.0005 nm against a decoder that was perfectly correct — XTC quantises by design. The oracle has to be what the reference implementation **reads back**. Getting that backwards invites loosening the tolerance until real bugs fit through as well.
  XTC stays **read-only** deliberately: ChiSurf writes DCD, which is lossless, so an encoder would exist only to hand files to other tools and would have to reproduce the quantisation ladder exactly to be worth having. TRR is not written either — no call site needs it.

* **Correction: the DCD reader was not faster, until numba made it so** ([PRD-80](prds/prd-80.md)). The commit that landed the codec (`1d6ed0493`) claimed "write 22 ms and read 5 ms against mdtraj's 34 ms and 14 ms". That came from a **single unrepeated measurement** and it was wrong — exactly the trap this project already has a note about. Measured properly (medians of 7 alternating runs, after a warm-up) the frame-by-frame reader was **0.79–1.04×**, i.e. slightly *slower* than the C plugin, and worst where its per-frame Python cost dominates: many frames of few atoms.
  **The fix is one numba pass.** The decoding was never the cost — a DCD payload is already `float32` — the per-frame seek, read and three strided assignments in Python were. Reading the whole payload once and de-interleaving X/Y/Z into `(frame, atom, 3)` in a single `prange` kernel gives, on the same repeated measurement: 200f×2500a **1.10×**, 464f×5235a **1.69×**, 2000f×500a **3.37×**, 50f×20000a **1.08×**. The biggest win is the many-frames case, which is where the old shape hurt most.
  **The A/B also produced the strongest correctness result available**, and it needs no other library at test time: reading the coordinates out of an mdtraj-written DCD and writing them back reproduces its coordinate records **byte for byte** — 1392 of 1392 on the full 464-frame trajectory, same md5. That says the reader and writer are exact *inverses* of the reference implementation's, which no tolerance comparison can say. It also explains the one apparent discrepancy: comparing against mdtraj's own array shows ~7.6e-06, which is **mdtraj's** Å→nm→Å conversion, not our error. That byte-for-byte check is now a committed test.

## 2026-08-05

* **ChiSurf reads and writes DCD itself, and it is faster than the C plugin** ([PRD-80](prds/prd-80.md)). First step of retiring mdtraj: `chisurf/core/fio/trajectory/dcd.py`, ported from VMD's `dcdplugin.c` — the **permissively licensed** (UIUC) C reference, not mdtraj's LGPL `.pyx` wrapper — to NumPy rather than a compiled extension, since ChiSurf is Cython-free. A frame is three contiguous `float32` blocks, so reading one is a `np.frombuffer`. On 2500 atoms × 200 frames: **write 22 ms and read 5 ms, against mdtraj's 34 ms and 14 ms** — one read plus a `frombuffer` per frame beats a `fread` per record.
  **The parity fixtures are committed, not generated, and that is the point.** A self-round-trip proves almost nothing about a binary interchange format: a reader and writer that share a misunderstanding — wrong endianness, a missed record marker, the cell fields in the wrong order — agree perfectly with each other and with nobody else. So `test/data/atomic_coordinates/trajectory/dcd/` now holds real DCD files written by mdtraj from this project's own test trajectory, with mdtraj's own coordinates alongside as the oracle, so the check outlives mdtraj. The triclinic fixture has three unequal lengths and three non-90 angles on purpose — an orthogonal cell hides an ordering mistake.
  **The unit cell is where this format bites.** Six values stored interleaved as `(A, gamma, B, beta, alpha, C)`, and as *cosines* in CHARMM/NAMD > 2.5 but as *degrees* in NAMD 2.5, with no flag to say which — a reader tells them apart by whether all three fall inside [-1, 1]. Both paths are covered, and the decodings were **mutation-tested**: swapping alpha/gamma, taking the lengths as values 0–2, and skipping the cosine branch are each caught. (A fourth mutation, `arccos` for `90 − asin`, is *not* caught and should not be — the two are the same identity; VMD prefers the latter only for its rounding at exactly 90°.)
  Also handled because real files use them: 64-bit record markers (CHARMM `-i8`), opposite-endian files, and the X-PLOR header variant. Refused loudly rather than mis-read: fixed-atom files, which store every atom only in frame 0 and would otherwise return the wrong coordinates silently. Units are **Ångström as stored** — nothing rescaled, because the other convention here is nanometres and a silent factor of ten in a FRET distance looks plausible.
  `.h5` trajectories are dropped outright rather than converted: they were an artefact of `TrajectoryFile` writing everything to HDF5, not a format anyone chose. XTC and TRR are next; mdtraj is cloned into `junk/` and recorded in `clone.sh` as the port source.

* **PRD-80 written: retiring `mdtraj` is the only way to be rid of `pytables` and `numexpr`** ([PRD-80](prds/prd-80.md)). The chain is `chisurf → mdtraj → pytables → numexpr`, both hard requirements — verified in the installed conda metadata rather than inferred. No ChiSurf module imports either directly any more, so nothing smaller than removing mdtraj will do it.
  **MDAnalysis was measured and rejected.** Standalone conda-forge closures: mdtraj **70**, MDAnalysis **142**, IMP **159**. It is twice the footprint, reintroduces `networkx` and `tqdm` (both retired here with a guardrail banning them), and does not read the format ChiSurf has on disk — its H5MD reader is not mdtraj's HDF5. It would take `pytables`/`numexpr` with it, at +72 packages net.
  **IMP has no DCD reader**, read from `../imp` rather than from the API listing: `modules/atom/include/` holds exactly `pdb.h`, `mmcif.h`, `mol2.h` and `secondary_structure_reader.h`, and every `dcd` match in the tree is prose about *citing* a DCD file in a deposition. A DCD codec is therefore the one genuinely new piece of code — the rest is porting.
  **The scope is far narrower than a grep suggests, which is the finding that makes this tractable.** mdtraj's HDF5 trajectory format is used in **exactly one file** (`core/structure/trajectory.py`); the 143 `.h5` references are that one class converting everything to HDF5 on construction. The other **24** `.h5` users are TTTR photons, bursts, H2MM and MMFDB and are untouched — and `hdf5` stays in the environment regardless, for the photon readers. Two more things shrink it: `compute_dssp` is only a *test oracle* for chimol's own secondary structure, not a runtime need, and Kabsch superposition is already in-tree.
  **Storing trajectories as RMF3 was the plan, and the measurement killed it.** On 2500 atoms x 200 frames: DCD writes in 34 ms and reads in **14 ms**; RMF3 writes in 4.0 s and reads in **10.5 s** through RMF's own `ParticleFactory` — 41.6 s through an IMP hierarchy — in a *larger* file. Bypassing IMP still costs 10.5 s, so this is RMF's per-node key model, not IMP overhead: right for a coarse-grained integrative model with richly annotated particles, wrong for a dense all-atom coordinate block. So **DCD holds frames and RMF3 holds hierarchies**. One good thing confirmed on the way: RMF3 is Avro-backed, not HDF5 (`Obj\x01…av`; `rmf-hdf5` is a separate deprecated suffix), so using it does not drag the HDF5 stack back in. And mdtraj *writes* DCD, which makes both the migration converter and the independent-reader test fixtures nearly free.
  Two open questions are recorded rather than assumed away: **IMP is imported 34 times but declared in no manifest** (allowlisted as a sibling project, with one *module-level* `IMP.cgmol` import), so whether a packaged install may depend on it decides whether the PRD is viable at all; and the eventual package saving must be **measured, not asserted** — an attempt during this investigation produced unusable output and was abandoned rather than reported.
