* **`ray` was far darker than the viewport: a missing term, not a missing setting** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Reported as "way too dark, and the lighting does not correspond to the live view" — one fault, not two. PyMOL's traced brightness has **two** diffuse terms: `bright = ambient + direct*direct_cmp + lreflect*reflect_cmp`, where `direct_cmp = pow(surfnormal[2], power)` is the normal's z in *camera* space — so `direct` is a **headlight**, lighting whatever faces the viewer regardless of the lamps. chimol had only the lamp term, so its ceiling was `ambient + diffuse` = **0.59** against PyMOL's ~1.0. (The averaging over lights was already right: `lreflect` carries `reflect_scale`, commented in the source as "divide up the reflected light component over all lights".) Measured on 148L's cartoon against the GL viewport, same scene and camera: mean lit **35.5 → 50.3**, viewport **51.1** — from 30 % below it to within 2 %. `direct` (0.45) and `power` (1.0) registered under PyMOL's names and defaults (`SettingInfo.h` 8, 11); new config keys, so no migration.
  **Not established and left as a lead:** whether the two also disagree about *framing*. A first look suggested the traced molecule sits smaller, but the viewport capture includes the panel and mouse-mode text drawn inside the GL widget and a brightness threshold counts those as molecule — the measurement was measuring chrome. Redo masked to the scene column, comparing silhouette boxes.

* **`ray` looked slow, and it was compiling, not tracing** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Reported as "1f5n takes more than 10 s". The trace is **0.4–0.6 s** for that structure at 638×291 2×2, and 0.46 s end-to-end through the command, thread and PNG write in a fresh process. The 10–33 s is **numba compiling the tracer**, cached under `~/.chisurf/cache/<module>_<contenthash>/` — and the hash is over the source, so *every* edit to `raytracer.py` or `bvh.py` discards the cache and the next `ray` pays a full recompile. Measured: **33.5 s** immediately after a kernel signature changed, **0.46 s** in the next fresh process; a fresh install pays it once. With nothing said that reads as "ray is slow", and the number reported back is the compile — so `ray` now announces the compile when `_jit_trace` has no signatures yet, and reports elapsed time in its "wrote" message either way.

* **Fitted Gaussian ellipses vanished a moment after being drawn — the 2-D overlay is one surface with three producers** ([PRD-56](prds/prd-56.md)). The companion tool's `overlay_plot` is a single painter widget; the equation curves, the Gaussian ellipses and the server-fed LineSets all paint onto it, and only the equation curves cleared it — unqualified. `_redraw_gaussian_overlays_from_table` then closed the loop itself: it drew the ellipses and scheduled a full `update_plots` **1 ms later** ("Trigger resize / otherwise plot flipped ? - Ugly fix"), which redrew the equation overlays, which cleared the whole surface. Measured on a two-blob fixture: 6 curves after the redraw, **0** after one turn of the event loop.
  **Curves now carry a layer** (`equations`, `gaussian`, `server:<tag>`) and `clear_curves(layer)` removes only that producer's work; a bare `clear_curves()` still means "everything" and stays for `clear_plots`. The LineSet store drops its per-tuple bookkeeping (it removed by value, and a tuple holding arrays cannot be compared — the removal would have silently stopped working) in favour of dropping its layer.
  **The deferred update was papering over a geometry bug**, so it is gone rather than guarded: the overlay froze each curve into *pixels* at `add_curve` time, so a resize — or the margins arriving after the curve did — left it describing a viewport that no longer existed. Mapping happens at paint time now, and a resize keeps the ellipses on their blobs. Leaving the timer in would have been worse than before: with the refresh path below it recurses forever (found by the test suite hanging).
  **Bin coordinates die with the histogram**, so `_refresh_curve_overlays` — the one place a new histogram becomes the displayed image — now redraws *all three* layers, not just the equation curves; `phasor_integration` keeps its source overlay dicts so its LineSets can be re-mapped there too.
  **`Histogram1D`/`2D`/`3D` are unpackable again.** Two computation paths reach `_histogram`, one storing tuples and one storing these containers, and ~15 readers spell it `H, x_edges, y_edges = ndx._histogram["2d"]` inside a bare `except` — against a container that raised `TypeError`, so the overlay was not drawn *at all* and nothing said so. `__iter__` delegating to `as_tuple()` fixes every one of them at the source.
  Verified headlessly on a real window (fit → update_plots → resize → equation-curve redraw → clear), screenshots inspected: ellipses centred on both blobs at 1σ/2σ/3σ, surviving every step, coexisting with an equation line. New: `test/test_overlay_layers.py` (7) and `test/test_gaussian_overlay_survives_redraw.py` (5, driving the real window). Full ndX suite **553 passed, 6 skipped**.

* **`numexpr` retired: its one expression is a Numba kernel, 22× faster** ([build/env](workflows/build-and-env.md)). The whole dependency existed for a single line in the dye-diffusion quenching code — `ne.evaluate('sum(k_quench * collided,axis=1)')` — plus an `ne.set_num_threads()` at import. The replacement reduces each frame's row on its own thread and never materialises the `(n_frames, n_atoms)` product, which for a long trajectory against a whole protein's quenching atoms is the largest array in the calculation: on 200 000 × 400, **634.7 ms → 29.2 ms** (plain NumPy is 316.7 ms). It is also the *more* accurate of the two — numexpr accumulated in float32 because `k_quench` is float32.
  **The thread setting went with it.** `n_threads` had exactly one reader, that `set_num_threads` call, and porting it literally would have been worse than deleting it: `numba.set_num_threads()` is process-wide, so a leaf module would have been re-configuring every parallel kernel in ChiSurf at import. Numba's thread count already comes from the `threads:` section via `env_bootstrap`, before Numba is imported. The key is gone from the shipped settings and the docs point at `threads:` instead.
  **Removing it frees no packages, and the entry says so.** `pytables` hard-requires `numexpr` (`tables/file.py` does `import numexpr as ne`), so it is installed either way. The declaration was still wrong to keep — we no longer import it — but this is a case where "dropped a dependency" would have overstated the result.
  Guardrail extended, as for the others.

## 2026-08-05

* **`pyarrow` and `boost-histogram` leave the manifests** ([build/env](workflows/build-and-env.md)). Neither was ever imported by ChiSurf: both were declared here on ndxplorer's behalf, and ndxplorer has since dropped them — its Arrow backend is gone and histograms are filled in the TTTR library, which on a 256×256 fill of 2,000,000 points takes 4.9 ms against boost's 8.7 ms threaded. `pyarrow-core`, `pyarrow` and `boost-histogram` are removed from `pixi.toml`, `pyproject.toml` and the recipe.
  Both join the retired-dependency guardrail, and **writing the negative test is what earned its keep**: the packaging check matched only the *wheel* spelling, so a conda recipe re-declaring `pyarrow-core` would have sailed straight past it. Distribution aliases are now checked alongside the primary name. The guardrail deliberately does **not** read the manifests under `modules/` — those are sibling checkouts this repository does not pin, so asserting on them would make the result depend on which revision of a neighbour happens to be on disk; each of those projects guards its own.
  Worth knowing for the next removal: the `bh.` in the Becker-Hickl readers is a block-header local, not `boost_histogram`. A name-based sweep flags it and the import regex must not.

## 2026-08-05

* **A cartoon casts a shadow now, and the WebGL viewer is read out** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). `ray_shadow` did nothing on the display chimol and PyMOL both start with: the shadow query walked a **sphere-only** tree, so a cartoon — zero spheres — reported every point fully lit, and a helix lying across another did not darken it. PyMOL shadows every primitive. The second tree was an optimisation from when a shadow ray cost a sweep of the whole scene; with the BVH it is one more descent of a tree that already exists, **so the fix deletes code rather than adding it** — one tree for both ray kinds, and `skip` becomes the hit primitive's unified index, finally correct for a triangle as well as a sphere. Cost on 148L at 320×240 2×2: cartoon 0.05 → 0.07 s, sticks 0.04 → 0.08 s, surface 0.07 → 0.12 s — 40–70 % more, from a base 100× faster than this morning. Checked for self-shadow acne, the failure mode this class of change has: none, and the difference sits in the crevices between surface lobes and under the ribbons, which is where a cast shadow belongs. 91 passed.
* **The WebGL viewer (`junk/ngl`) is read out, and its checkout is deleted.** Surveyed the whole tree, not only the shaders. What it was consulted for is captured: the five shader techniques are transcribed into the tracker, and one of the five was **measured and rejected** (impostors buy ~1 ms on an ordinary molecule). Everything else duplicates an authority chimol already has and the authority is better — its representations (`rocket`, `unitcell`, `slice`, `hyperball`), colour schemes (hydrophobicity, occupancy, partial charge, B-factor) and measurements all exist in PyMOL under names chimol is *required* to match, so taking them from NGL would mean implementing the right feature under the wrong name and defaults. Two things neither PyMOL nor ChimeraX has are written down so dropping the checkout does not lose them: an EDT-based solvent-excluded surface (a third algorithm again — PyMOL's is the one to match), and a flat spatial hash that `geometry/neighbors.py` already implements. **PyMOL stays the authority on behaviour, ChimeraX on rendering quality; NGL was only ever the third opinion on shaders.** The 1.0 GB checkout is **deleted**, and two things were done so the deletion sticks and costs nothing: the tracker now carries the upstream URL and the exact commit everything was read from (`60be69b5`), since the shader notes cite paths inside it; and `junk/clone.sh` — which re-clones every reference tree and would have silently restored it on the next run — carries the decision instead of the clone line.

* **The viewport had no depth cue, and PyMOL's settings for it were pointed at the tracer** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). `depth_cue`, `fog` and `fog_start` are *global* in PyMOL — `SceneSetFog` applies them to the viewport and the tracer follows unless `ray_trace_fog`/`ray_trace_fog_start` override, which is why those two names exist. chimol registered all three against `ray.*` and applied them only to the tracer, so the interactive view had **no depth cue at all** and the traced image disagreed with the viewport it reproduces. The shader was already written for it: `fogDensity`, `fogColor`, the uniform lookup and the fragment `mix` were all in place, and `self._fog_density = 0.0` in `__init__` was **the only assignment in the tree** — a complete feature held off by one initialiser, and the fourth thing this session that was built and unreachable.
  Both halves transcribed rather than invented. **Shape:** PyMOL's fog is *linear between two planes*, `fog = (g_Fog_end + eye_pos.z) * g_Fog_scale` in `data/shaders/default.vs`, a **visibility** with scale `1/(end − start)`; chimol's shader had `1 − exp(−density·|viewPos|)`, a different curve that makes `fog_start` mean nothing. **Planes:** `FogStart = (back − front)·fog_start + front`, `FogEnd = FogStart + (back − FogStart)/fog` for `fog` in (0,1) else `back`, with front/back fitted **around the scene** (camera distance ± target radius) rather than the camera's far plane — the identical distinction the tracer's fog fix turned on, where getting it wrong fogged every pixel 24–69 % with none left unfogged. Defaults are PyMOL's: `depth_cue` on, `fog` 1.0, `fog_start` 0.45.
  Measured on 148L as spheres: **91.6 % of lit pixels unfogged**, recessed ones down to 0.48. The guardrail asserts **both halves of that pair** — something fogged *and* something not — because a dimmer passes either one alone, which is precisely how the tracer's fog failure survived a single-number check. `_fog_planes` reads the config every frame rather than caching onto the renderer, so `set depth_cue, off` cannot leave a stale copy — the failure the silhouette settings still have. 128 passed across the render and settings tests.
  Recorded and not done: the config path is still `ray.depth_cue` / `ray.fog_start` / `ray.fog_intensity`, which reads wrong for settings governing both renderers. Moving them is a **key move** and the migration table only knows how to update a *default*, so it needs a small loader extension — worth doing together with `silhouette`'s two-store problem.


* **Silhouettes were built and unusable: switching them on deleted the sequence strip and moved the molecule** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). The tracker named the render-to-texture scaffolding as the *next task*; it has been there for some time with silhouettes on top of it — another stated gap with a shelf life. What was true is that nobody could have used it. Three defects, all where the offscreen pass meets the rest of the frame, all invisible to the suite because nothing rendered a *window* with an effect on: (1) `_render_overlay` paints with QPainter, which targets the **widget's** framebuffer rather than the bound one, and it ran *before* the composite, so the blit erased the chrome — the strip lost **53 %** of its ink (the two early-return paths in `paintGL` already had the right order; only the path that draws a molecule did not); (2) the offscreen buffer took the window's full height while the direct path reserves a band for the strip, so the scene rendered centred in a taller frame and visibly shifted, and the blit covered the band too; (3) a window that has not been laid out built a **1-pixel-wide** framebuffer — the same `scene_width` floor that once told the camera the window was thirty times taller than wide — so the composite blitted a one-pixel column and **the molecule disappeared**. The effect passes now decline below `_MIN_MEASURABLE_SCENE`.
  **The metric lied before the picture did.** The first measurement read "10.28 % of pixels changed — the setting works." It did change the picture: it was deleting the strip and moving the molecule. A real outline moves **0.15 %**, and that ratio is now the assertion, because here *more* change is the failure. Same lesson the two-sided-lighting work recorded, reached from the opposite direction.
  Guardrails in `test_lighting.py`, which already renders real framebuffers; both checked against the old code and they do fail there. The strip one asserts **ink coverage** rather than pixel equality — painting after a composite leaves QPainter different GL state and shifts glyph antialiasing by up to 12/255 (mean 0.38) with the crops indistinguishable, while erasure takes the ink to nearly nothing. The third defect caught the *test* before the code: a window restored from a persisted dock layout handed the 3-D widget 109×350, under the panel's own 220-pixel column, so the helper forces a viewport and **asserts** it got one instead of skipping.
  Recorded and not done: `set silhouette, on` is not a registered setting, so the feature is reachable only via the ChimeraX-style `lighting silhouette=on`; and `set_lighting` writes `_post` directly while `_DISPLAY_CONFIG["silhouette"]` is read only at construction — two stores for one state, so registering the name means fixing that first or shipping one more setting that stores and does nothing.


* **Every ChiMOL frame rebuilt the whole scene, through a colour query: surface 82 ms → 4.25 ms** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). `paintGL` → `_render_overlay` → `_refresh_gui_state` → `get_residue_colors` → **`_build_scene_for_current_object`**. The sequence strip has no signal telling it that `color`/`spectrum`/`ss` ran, so it re-reads the residue colours every frame — reasonable — but the only way to get them ran the entire scene builder: with a surface shown, a density grid, marching cubes, gradients and ambient occlusion **sixty times a second**. 148L at 1280×860: surface **82.12 → 4.25 ms** (12 → 235 fps), cartoon 28.34 → 4.12, spheres 17.34 → 4.94, sticks 11.61 → 3.91. The colour half is split out as `_recompute_colors_per_ca`, which is all `get_residue_colors` calls now.
  **The measurement is the transferable part.** Frame time was *flat against pixel count* — 8× the pixels, same milliseconds — which rules out fill work and vertex work in one experiment and says the cost is fixed CPU work per frame. That is what redirected the search from the shaders to the profiler. **Ask a frame to scale before assuming what it spends on.** The call site carried the comment *"Reading them back is a cached array copy, which costs nothing beside drawing the molecule itself"* — it was the most expensive thing in the frame, and that comment is why nobody looked. **A comment asserting a cost is a claim with a shelf life.**
  One hazard the split introduced and the fix closes: `get_residue_colors` sized its array from `self._coords.shape[0]`, which on a **trajectory** is the frame count, not the residue count. The old code got away with it because the rebuild set the array correctly and a shape check then rejected the *return value*; computing it directly would have stored a wrongly-sized array on the viewer for the renderer to read. `_ca_coords_2d` is now the one definition, and is read-only so a colour query cannot advance a trajectory. Guardrail is structural, not timed, and was checked against the old code to confirm it fails there.
  **This also settles the impostor question rather than leaving it open.** With the rebuild gone, 210 240 vertices cost 0.9 ms more per frame than 5 536, so cylinder/sphere impostors have about a millisecond to win on an ordinary molecule against a ~3.9 ms floor that is the sequence strip's *text*. They stay right above `impostor_min_atoms` (20 000), which is what they were added for. Where a cylinder primitive would still pay is the **ray tracer**, replacing the tessellated 8-sided shafts with an exact primitive — the trade `meta["spheres"]` already makes for balls.


* **The system-info overlay moves to the bottom left, and is off by default** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). The top left of the viewport is where the sequence strip and the object panel already put text, and a framed structure sits centre-high, so an overlay anchored there competed with both. **`MolView._info_visible` already started `False`** — the toolbar button was constructed `checked=True` and switched it back on at startup, so the shipped default was the opposite of the one the viewer declared. Nothing tested either fact; two guardrails added in `test_panel_layout.py`, measuring the anchor rather than asking whether the widget exists.
  Two things measured on the way. `info_overlay.full_height` **has no effect**: `addWidget` is given an alignment, so the widget takes its size hint rather than the cell, and the row span the flag controls changes nothing (192 px tall in a 631 px container either way) — left alone rather than changed, since changing a shipped default costs a config migration and this one buys nothing. And the screenshot helper **pastes the GL framebuffer over the widget area**, which hides any overlay child sitting on the 3-D view: a whole-window grab showed no info panel at all while it was plainly visible. Grabbing the container instead shows both.

* **Shader techniques surveyed from a WebGL viewer, none taken yet** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). `junk/ngl/src/shader/` read for *how* while PyMOL stays the authority on *what*. The headline: ChiMOL draws spheres as impostors only past 20 000 atoms, so an ordinary molecule gets tessellated sticks — **33 216 triangles on 148L** for what is a few hundred capped cylinders — where a cylinder impostor ray-casts them exactly from one quad, faster and without facets at any zoom. Four smaller ones, each a handful of lines: interior colouring so a clipped surface reads as solid rather than hollow (the same `gl_FrontFacing` hook `two_sided_lighting` already added), opaque back faces as the cheap half of order-independent transparency, SDF glyphs for labels that survive zoom, and a matrix-scale helper so an impostor radius survives a scaled transform. Recorded with what each buys, in the rendering section.


* **`ray` was 143–651× slower than it needed to be; every ray tested every primitive** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). The tracer had no acceleration structure: each sample intersected every sphere and every triangle in the scene, for every transparency layer. A cartoon is 39 252 triangles and a solvent surface 51 748, so a publication-sized render — 1024×768, 2×2 samples — cost **195 s**. It now costs **0.30 s**. Measured on 148L at 320×240 2×2: cartoon 19.12 s → 0.126 s (151×), sticks 8.96 → 0.062 (144×), surface 35.00 → 0.198 (177×), lines 51.11 → 0.152 (337×). A binned-SAH BVH in `renderer/bvh.py`, with spheres and triangles in one index space so a mixed scene is one tree and one descent.
  **The earlier 380× sphere-mesh fix was the same bug seen through a keyhole.** Trading 210 240 triangles for 1363 spheres worked because cost was linear in the primitive count per ray — which meant it could not generalise to any representation whose triangles are not secretly spheres. `spheres` gains least here (5.6×) precisely because it was the one case already treated. **A speedup that large is rarely a property of the geometry; it is usually the complexity class.**
  **The picture is unchanged, and that was differenced rather than assumed.** cartoon, sticks and surface are **bit-identical**, every pixel. `spheres` (3.6 % of pixels) and `lines` (0.03 %) differ because the tree exposed a defect it did not cause: the shadow query returned **whichever occluder came first in the array**, so contact-shadow softness depended on scene build order. PyMOL takes the nearest, and only when the decay is on — `nearest_shadow = (shadow_decay != _0)`, `layer1/Ray.cpp` — because the decay is a function of occluder distance. All 2 788 changed pixels are **brighter, none darker**, which is what the nearest occluder implies under `occlusion = 1 − exp(−(t − decay_range)·decay)` and is how the change was confirmed to be that one change alone. A second defect fell out beside it: the hit primitive was passed as the sphere to skip **without checking it was a sphere**, so a triangle hit stopped one sphere from casting — invisible except on a mixed scene, which is what a wireframe is.
  **Two traps, both of which draw a plausible wrong picture rather than failing.** A cartoon is full of exactly axis-aligned triangles whose bounding box is exactly flat, and a ray in that plane computes `0 × inf`; the NaN loses every comparison and the triangle silently leaves the image, so bounds are padded at build time. And a traversal stack that overflows drops geometry, so the build caps depth and forces an over-full leaf instead — slow is the right way for that to fail.
  **The guardrail that matters is the cost one.** Every correctness test in `test/test_bvh.py` passes just as well against an exhaustive search, so removing the tree would leave a green suite; cost is asserted separately, at a resolution where the trace and not the (linear) tree build dominates. Benchmark: `test/benchmarks/benchmark_chimol_ray.py`.
  Recorded and not fixed: **nothing but a sphere casts a shadow** — the shadow tree holds spheres only, so on a cartoon-only display `ray_shadow` does nothing at all. Unaffordable before, affordable now, and a rendering decision rather than a performance one; the seam and what it would change are in the parity concept.

* **`tifffile`, `imageio` and `imagecodecs` are gone; there is one image seam** ([image IO](subsystems/image-io.md), [build/env](workflows/build-and-env.md)). Three dependencies existed to read TIFF stacks, which the TTTR library already does with a bundled, statically-linked libtiff — no runtime dependency of its own. Every call site now goes through `chisurf.core.fio.image` (`imread`/`imwrite`/`read_labelled`/`metadata`). Verified bit-for-bit against `tifffile` on the real LZW-compressed `RICS_EGFPGFP.tif`.
  **TIFF is the only format, in both directions.** Measurement images are TIFF: full-depth integer and float pixel types, lossless, carrying the axis and voxel-size metadata that makes a stack interpretable. The consumer formats store 8-bit colour, so writing a 16-bit photon count or a float lifetime map into one silently discards the measurement — the seam raises rather than converting, and refuses to *read* them for the same reason, since a PNG in that position means the data was flattened upstream. Pillow stays a ChiSurf dependency but no longer touches data: ChiMOL's render export and the docs tooling are pictures, not measurements. ndxplorer's mask I/O went the same way — its save dialog had offered PNG beside TIFF — and now depends on tttrlib directly.
  **The dependency count was the smaller half.** Each reader answered a different question about the same file: a TIFF is a flat page sequence, so six pages cannot say whether they are six frames or two frames in three colours, and the guesses disagreed. `read_labelled` returns the axis labels, and a plain stack is reported as `"IYX"` — *unlabelled* pages — rather than `"TYX"`, so a guess never travels downstream as if it had been read from disk.
  **Upstream (tttrlib, `b7b25179` + `1adff541`).** `TiffInfo` carries the raw `ImageDescription` and resolution tags and `write_tiff` accepts them; the Python layer reads and writes ImageJ hyperstack metadata, so `imwrite(path, stack, axes="TCYX")` round-trips a 4-D array and `imwrite(..., resolution=…, metadata={"spacing":…, "unit":…})` gives a z-stack a physical voxel size. Round-trip *and* cross-reader agreement checked for `CYX`/`TYX`/`TCYX`/`ZCYX`/`TZCYX`. Two things the tests pin that a shape check would miss: the page order is channel-fastest, so a reader reshaping in the wrong order still returns the right dimensions; and a description that does not multiply out to the pages on disk is ignored rather than used to scramble the stack.
  **One behaviour is strictly better than what it replaced.** `tifffile` writes a `(4, y, x)` float array as *one page with four samples per pixel*, labels it `"SYX"`, and a four-frame movie comes back as an RGBA-like image — a trap documented in three separate places in this tree. The bundled writer writes four pages.
  **Two defects found on the way, both silent.** `skimage.io` reads through an imageio plugin, so two `except ImportError` fallbacks to it would have become dead paths rather than errors — the guardrail test now bans `skimage.io` by name alongside the three packages. And tttrlib's own `CLSMSuperRes._read_tiff` still imported `tifffile` and raised "needs the 'tifffile' package" on installations that had TIFF support compiled in all along.
  Not fixed here and written down instead: `img_flow`'s demo PTU reconstructs **29 of its 30 frames** — 30 frame markers and 1920/1920 line markers are all present in the stream. Unrelated to this change, and invisible to the default suite because the test is marked `slow`; measurement and where the frame goes are in [known issues](references/known-issues.md).

* **Numba is required across ChiMOL; the unexercised NumPy twins are gone** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Ten modules carried `_HAVE_NUMBA` with a pure-NumPy sibling behind it. Nothing ran those siblings while numba was installed -- which is exactly how the ray tracer's twin came to be **silently broken**: the transparency work landed in both, the NumPy one referenced a parameter it did not take, and every test still passed. A fallback nobody runs is not a safety net but an untested branch. ~600 lines removed, along with the `except Exception: pass` handlers that quietly downgraded a jit failure to a slower path.
  Three kinds of code needed telling apart, and mixing them up was the easy mistake: **tests of the deleted branch** were removed (two in `test_trajectory_performance.py` that forced `_HAVE_NUMBA = False`); **tests merely guarded by the flag** kept their assertions and lost the guard (the cell-list-vs-brute-force AO comparison); and **NumPy code used as a test oracle** stayed (`_occlusion_from_spheres_numpy`, the only independent check on that kernel). `bonds.py` kept its NumPy path too -- its guard was `_HAVE_NUMBA and nb is not None and n > 1`, where `n > 1` is a real condition.
  **Two self-inflicted process lessons.** A bulk regex edit with `re.S` matched from each file's *first* `try:`, which in `cartoon.py` was the sibling-import block, not the numba one -- so three imports vanished and every cartoon test failed with a `NameError` far from the cause. The verification that caught it had to compare **every name the module binds, imports included**; an earlier scan over top-level *definitions* reported clean and was wrong. And twice a long suite run was invalidated by editing the tree while it ran: a running suite makes the tree read-only.

* **The RPC server could not build a fit at all** ([headless server](architecture/server.md)). `fit_create` resolves a model by walking `Model.__subclasses__()`, which only sees *imported* classes — and the server imports none of them. Measured in a fresh server process: **exactly one** model class reachable ("Global fit", pulled in by the fitting machinery), so every `fit.create` naming a real model answered `model 'X' not found`. Running the same headless bootstrap the agent layer already uses (`ensure_experiments_registered`) takes it to **43**, and the error now lists what is available.
  **Two more defects were hidden behind that one**, each reachable only once the first was fixed: `FitGroup` *iterates* its data to build one member fit per dataset, and a bare `DataCurve` iterates into `(x, y)` tuples — so the single-dataset path built member fits whose `data` was a tuple and the first read of `data.x` failed; and a server-created fit had the range `(0, 0)`, so it could be created but never run (`Improper input: N=4 must not exceed M=(0,)`). Fixing one at a time is how they surfaced — each was invisible behind the one before it.
  Also: `fit_set_dataset` did not accept `fit_uid` while the dispatcher passes it, and `fit_set_result_idx` made `fit_index` a required positional, so addressing either **by uid — the documented way — raised `TypeError` inside the dispatcher**. And `Fit.set_result_idx` documented "clipped to the valid range" while `np.clip(idx, 0, len(results) - 1)` returns **-1** for an empty deque and then indexes it: "this fit has not been run yet" reached the caller as `IndexError: deque index out of range`.
  `test_integration_lifecycle.py`: **51 failed / 23 passed → 43 failed / 31 passed**. The remainder is a *test-isolation* problem rather than 43 separate faults — the file shares one module-scoped server and resets only datasets and fits, and `TestErrorBoundary` passes **12/12 alone** but fails 3 in the full file. Resume point and the traps in measuring it: [headless server](architecture/server.md); the port pattern for the stale `{"ok": False}` contract is in [known issues](references/known-issues.md).
  **A correction worth keeping**: this suite was first reported as *deadlocked*, on the strength of a stack sample showing `zmq_ctx_destroy`. The sample was accurate and the conclusion was not — the block was real only while fits could not be created. The file now runs to completion; its 13.5 minutes are repeated client timeouts. A sampled stack says where a process is, not that it is stuck: check whether CPU time is advancing.

* **`ray` walks through a translucent surface** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Each ray now composites front to back instead of stopping at the nearest hit, so the traced image shows the cartoon inside a glass shell exactly as the viewport does. **Free when unused**: on 148L at 300x220, opaque renders in 3.60 s with four layers allowed against 3.83 s with one, because the walk ends at the first solid hit; translucent is 9.06 s, 2.4x rather than 4x, because it also stops once the remaining transmittance cannot change a byte.

Replaced with two spheres driven through `trace()` directly, where red can only reach the centre pixel through the shell, plus the converse that an opaque shell must not leak it.

## 2026-08-05

* **`surface_quality` was three defects wearing one name** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Flagged as a units wart -- PyMOL takes a level, chimol a grid spacing -- and each measurement found something worse underneath. **It is not a different quantity**: `RepSurfaceSetSettings` shows the level *selects* a point separation in Angstrom, which is what chimol stores; the eight levels and four base separations are transcribed, the bases registered because the table reads them. **Then the level did nothing** -- levels -3 to 1 moved 148L from 26 286 to 27 238 vertices, 3.6 % across an eightfold request, because `max_dim` caps the grid at 96 samples/axis and *rescales the spacing to fit*. **Then the reason turned out to be worse**: `_all_atom_coords` is in scene units (Angstrom x 10) and the spacing was passed through as if it were too, so `0.8` asked for **0.08 A** and the cap clamped it back. The spacing had never had a measurable effect; `max_dim` was making the whole decision. `add_volume` already converts -- one path forgot what its neighbour remembers.
  Fixed: 2 446 / 13 654 / 25 876 / 105 922 vertices at levels -3 / -1 / 0 / 1 (43x, monotone, and visibly different). The shipped default moves 0.8 -> 0.5 A by config migration 7 -> 8, which **changes the number without changing the picture**: honest 0.8 would have made every existing surface coarser than users see, while 0.5 is PyMOL's own `surface_normal`, is `surface_quality 0`, and reproduces today's appearance. 74 registered settings; `preset ligand_sites` now performs all four of PyMOL's steps with nothing skipped.
  **And a fourth, from the same thread:** `solvent_radius` was registered **twice**, onto two different config keys -- `surface.probe_radius` (which the surface mesh reads) and `surface.solvent_radius` (which `get_area` reads). The later entry silently shadows the earlier, so `set solvent_radius` moved the number the area calculation used and left the surface on screen untouched: one quantity, two storages, disagreeing quietly. Collapsed onto one key; the probe now moves the surface (34 770 / 30 744 / 25 260 vertices at 1.0 / 1.4 / 2.5 A). Two guardrails added -- no name registered twice, no one name writing several config entries (the reverse stays legal, since `cartoon_side_chain_helper` and `ribbon_side_chain_helper` are deliberately one setting).
  **Worth carrying: "the setting is registered" and "the setting works" are different claims.** Four defects sat behind one flagged wart -- wrong type, no effect, 10x units, two homes -- and each had a live config path, a passing test and a correct-looking name. Only measuring the output caught them.

* **ChiMOL sees through a surface: `transparency` and `two_sided_lighting`** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). The first and fourth names on the settings worklist, and the two `preset ligand_sites` had been reporting as skipped. **PyMOL counts transparency where chimol stores alpha, and they run opposite ways** -- `transparency 0` is opaque, `alpha 1` is -- so `SettingSpec` gained `stored`/`shown` transforms and the complement is declared once rather than kept as two numbers that must agree. A guardrail asserts every transforming spec round-trips. `unset transparency` restores chimol's shipped 0.15, not PyMOL's 0: `unset` restores *the* default, and changing what this program ships is a config migration, not a settings entry. 70 registered settings, each read by code.
  **The picture caught what the tests could not.** Wiring the setting to the existing `twoSided` uniform passed every test and drew the wrong thing: that uniform flips the normal toward the *light* (written for flat nucleic base plates), while PyMOL's two-sided lighting flips a back face toward the *viewer*. Fixed with `gl_FrontFacing`, with the caveat recorded that on a closed surface the two criteria mostly coincide, so the measured difference is negligible -- a correctness fix for the failure mode it removes, not for a number.
  **And the first metric was wrong**, which is the part worth carrying. Mean brightness *fell* 7.6 % when two-sided lighting came on and that read as a bug; it is not, because the newly lit back faces are mid-grey and veil brighter cartoon pixels. Only the side-by-side images settled it. A scalar over the whole frame cannot tell "back faces now lit" from "bright cartoon now obscured", and picking the metric before looking is how a correct change gets reverted.

## 2026-08-05

* **Session close: the `?` + **Guide** pass, where it stands and what stopped it** ([help buttons and guided tours](subsystems/gui-help-and-guides.md), [known issues](references/known-issues.md)). Ten commits took the shrinking allow-list from **105 → 81** of the 109 plugins declaring a GUI entrypoint: the shared seam and its guard, the QA harness, and twenty tours written with real content — the burst pipeline, the whole FCS group, two of the decay group, four imaging tools, the RICS planner and the binned HMM.
  **What the pass was actually worth was not the count.** Six ways a tour could point at nothing while every automated check passed were found by *rendering it and looking*, and each is now fixed in shared code with a discriminating test: a closed dock tab, a stack orphaned by a layout rebuild, a folded `CollapsibleBox` (which re-folds itself mid-step unless `auto_fold` is suspended), a bubble covering its own target, a wizard whose heading did not follow the step, and — twice — the *static guard itself* accepting a name that existed somewhere in the view spec but resolved to nothing in the window. The pattern behind all six is one sentence: **a guard verifies that a name exists; only the render verifies that it points at the thing the reader is looking at.**
  Two rules came out of it and are written down rather than remembered. Legacy plotting you walk past is legacy you own — `.native` reaches pyqtgraph *without importing it*, so 12 files had slipped past the import guard, and most of them were never gaps at all ([chiplot](subsystems/chiplot.md)). And a toolbar carrying only `?` and **Guide** is chrome: a tool's primary actions belong on it, matched by the `action` its view spec names.
  **Stopped by the environment, not by the work.** Mid-session every GUI tool began failing with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tttrlib'` — the arm64 env's `tttrlib.py` and `_tttrlib…so` are symlinks into a pixi cache directory that had been emptied, and a dangling symlink imports as "no module". It is not repairable by relinking: `direct_url.json` shows the install came from `modules/tttrlib`, and the only build tree there has the SWIG wrapper but no compiled extension, so it needs a real rebuild. Left for the user to decide rather than compiled into their environment unasked, with no pixi running to coordinate with.
  **Left uncommitted on purpose:** `irf_estimator`'s `help.md`, `guide.json` and the `tool.py` change that deletes its `HelpDialog`. The static guard passes; the tour has never been walked. Committing a GUI change on the strength of the guard alone is precisely the mistake this session found six instances of, so it waits for the harness. The order is in the concept's resume section.

## 2026-08-04

* **Nine red tests, seven real defects** ([fitting](subsystems/fitting.md), [testing workflow](workflows/testing.md)). Ran the whole suite per directory (a directory-wide run dies with SIGBUS and takes the report with it) and fixed the root cause of each failure rather than the assertion.
  **A lifetime model started as N identical exponentials.** `Lifetime.append` gave every component the same 4 ns, so a two-exponential fit began with two Jacobian columns that are the *same vector* and nothing to separate them with. On the 10k-photon FRET sub-ensemble decay of `test/agent/test_burst_workflow.py` the fitted efficiency moved between **0.04 and 0.55** — every one at a reduced chi2 of 0.79-0.95 — depending on nothing but the lifetime bounds. Components now start `COMPONENT_SPACING` (3x) apart, and the same four bounds give 0.575, 0.579, 0.583, 0.572 with a *better* chi2 (0.77). The declared `[0.001, 100]` ns lifetime bounds were also never switched on (`bound_on` covered only the amplitudes), which is what let a fit reach tau = 393 ns with a time shift of -2663 channels; `bound_on_lifetime` defaults to on. Amplitudes stay unbounded — a negative amplitude is a rise term.
  **Attempted and reverted: bounding `bg` at zero.** The runaway *is* fixed by forbidding a negative background, and the argument looks sound (its sibling `sc` is bounded on the same grounds). It is wrong: `bg` is a *net offset*, not a count rate, and on data whose background is already subtracted the good fit genuinely wants it negative. Measured on the EasyTau300 reference decay, `bg >= 0` turned reduced chi2 **1.37 into 4.93**. Also reverted: nudging a parameter that *starts on* its bound to where the transform has a non-zero derivative. Both transforms are quadratically flat at a bound, so such a parameter really cannot move — but an offset large enough to help is, for a wide box, enormous in the parameter's own units (0.1 internal = 0.25% of the range = **millions** for a rate bounded at 1e9), and it broke three PDA rate tests. The flat-at-the-bound behaviour is real and remains, [documented](references/known-issues.md).
  **The ensemble samplers ignored the only seed a caller has.** `sample_ensemble`, `sample_ensemble_slice` and `sample_differential_evolution` built `np.random.default_rng(seed)`, which with `seed=None` draws fresh OS entropy and silently ignores `np.random.seed` — the very thing `_rng` exists to prevent, and its docstring says so. A sampling test failed about one run in four. All samplers route through `_rng`, which now returns a real `Generator` seeded from the global stream. `walk_mcmc` had also lost its `@frozen('fit', 'model')` decorator when `_rng` was inserted below it: the decorator stayed on the line above and ended up wrapping `_rng`, which has neither argument and froze nothing.
  **`fit.model = <a model>` raised `TypeError`.** The setter took only a class, so the getter's own return value was not accepted — `issubclass() arg 1 must be a class`. It now takes either, re-pointing an adopted model at this fit; the bare `type` placeholder stays a no-op because `FitGroup.__init__` passes it through to the selected member fit. And `FittingParameterGroup(parameters=[p])` lost `p` on the first rediscovery, because `find_parameters` clears `_parameters` before walking `__dict__`; constructor-supplied parameters are now kept.
  **Importing the settings editor corrupted every later `yaml.dump` in the process.** `yaml.add_representer(float, ...)` registers on the global `yaml.Dumper`, at import time, and the representer keeps ten decimal digits where a double needs seventeen: any project file or curve saved afterwards no longer round-tripped (`2.4492935982947064e-16` came back as `2.4492935983e-16`). Moved to a local `SettingsDumper`.
  **A second `QApplication` per process.** `get_app()` constructed one unconditionally; the second call is undefined behaviour and took the GUI suite down with a **segmentation fault**, which killed every later test in the run and left no report. It reuses the existing instance.
  **Write-only settings.** The acquisition simulator's `q_green_p`-style fields were still accepted but no longer read (`to_parameters` takes brightness from `species_q`), so configuring them did nothing at all; removed. The detector wizard's `json_file` loaded a *setups file* — the very file it saves — as if it were a single setup, producing a silently empty page; it now recognises both.
  **Six tests reached the real api.mistral.ai** because they stubbed `sys.modules["requests"]`, which the code stopped using when it moved to the in-tree `chisurf.core.http`. Ported to that seam, with a guard that fails on any unstubbed request. Test doubles also re-pointed at the current structure for the burst-background tool (AutoForm + Qt-free view model), the detector G-factor cell (which deliberately reverts programmatic writes) and the photon-filter page (whose Designer spin boxes are now a write-only mirror of `FilterSettings`).
  Suites: 1809 passed (agent, tcspc, fitting, models, decay) + 54 (gui/settings) + 12 (sampler seeding) + 6 (lifetime start) + 3 (settings dumper). Remaining GUI failures and the shared-environment breakage that blocked further verification are in [known issues](references/known-issues.md).

* **A toolbar carrying only `?` and Guide is chrome — the primary actions move onto it** ([help buttons and guided tours](subsystems/gui-help-and-guides.md)). The toolbar-less tools got a hairline strip so the pair had somewhere to live; a *Run* button buried three panels down a settings column and a bar with nothing on it are the same defect twice, and `promote_to_toolbar(form, toolbar, actions)` fixes both at once.
  Buttons are matched on the **`action` their view spec names**, never on their label — a label is a translation and a decoration away from changing; AutoForm's `ButtonRowWidget` already tags each button with `_autoform_action`, so no view spec had to change. The helper takes an **explicit list** rather than promoting everything it can find, because the judgement is per tool and belongs in the call: *Fit* / *Scan states* (hmm), *Generate* / *Save* (synthetic decay) and *Simulate + Correlate* (FLCS sim) are window-level actions; *Add row*, *Remove*, *Load* and *Apply to this field* stay in the form, where a section-scoped button means something.
  **The bug the render caught:** hiding a button's container once it held no more buttons is right for a `button_row` and wrong for a *custom* section — the FLCS simulator pairs its action with a status label, so the button moved to the toolbar and the line reporting the result vanished with it. The condition is now "nothing at all is left", not "no buttons left". Pinned by a test that builds both shapes.
  Also removed `core/hmm`'s inline `{"type": "custom", "key": "help"}` section: it opened the same `help.md` with the same title as the new toolbar `?`, so it was a second door to one room.
  Suites: 104(+9 skipped); all three tours re-walked clean.

* **The RICS-precision planner and the binned-trace HMM get their tours** ([help buttons and guided tours](subsystems/gui-help-and-guides.md)). Allow-list **83 → 81**; both already shipped `help.md`, so this exhausts the cheap "help exists, tour missing" set — every remaining plugin now needs both files written.
  **RICS precision** is the one tool in ChiSurf used *before* the measurement, and its tour says the awkward part plainly: where the optimum dwell lies depends on the D you are trying to measure, i.e. the number you do not have yet — so run it at both ends of your uncertainty rather than trusting one confident answer. It also carries the two honest limits into the tour: each point is itself a Monte-Carlo estimate (~10 % at the default repeat count), so the minimum is an order of magnitude and not a setting to dial in; and precision is quoted per *frame count*, not per unit time, so a slower scan in the comparison is also a longer acquisition.
  **HMM** is built around the fact that the likelihood cannot choose the state count — adding a state always improves it, so the elbow is not evidence — plus the three diagnostics that refute a fit and are all invisible in the likelihood: overlapping emission densities, a dwell-time histogram that curves on a log axis (one state that is really two), and a state with a mean dwell of one bin.
  **Finding: an inline `help` section had disguised a plugin as finished.** `core/hmm` declares `{"type": "custom", "key": "help"}` in its view spec and ships `help.md`, so it read as done — and the harness reported *no Guide button*, because nothing had ever added a toolbar to put one on. An AutoForm `help` section answers what a control means; it cannot answer which one to touch first, and it leaves the tour nowhere to live. The tool now gets the same hairline strip as the other toolbar-less ones.
  Suites: 78(+9 skipped); both tours walk clean (5 steps each); ruff clean.

* **ChiMOL's camera stays where you put it** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Every scene rebuild refitted it, and a rebuild is what colouring, a representation change, a label, a bond edit and **every** `set` all trigger. Measured on 148L: `zoom resi 20-26` frames at distance 357 and **12 of 12** ordinary commands put it straight back to 1730. `_update_view(fit_camera=...)` now defaults to `False`, with the three load paths passing `True` — PyMOL's `auto_zoom`, and nothing else.
  **This was recorded as attempted-and-reverted, and the recorded reason was a symptom seen through another defect.** The note said the flip was insufficient because `ray` then traced an empty image for every representation. It was not insufficient: the empty images were the `_aspect()` defect fixed earlier the same day — a never-shown window has no viewport, so the camera went 30x too far — and refitting on every rebuild hid it because the last rebuild landed after the widget had a size. With that fixed, the same flip passes `test_ray_command.py` untouched. **When an attempt fails, record what was measured, not what was concluded.**
  Two things it needed on top, both found by measuring: `_rebuild_after_coordinate_change` reuses `set_structure` — the *load* path — to re-derive after an edit, so `h_add` on a zoomed-in residue still jumped out until `set_structure`/`set_coordinates` grew a `fit_camera` argument; and nothing re-derived the distance on a **resize**, which the old behaviour had been covering by accident, so `resizeGL` re-frames when the viewport's shape changes (distance only — the clips carry a user's `clip` adjustments). That correction **scales** the distance rather than recomputing it: the scroll wheel moves the camera without touching what was framed, so recomputing would snap a hand-zoomed view back to the last `zoom`. The rule itself is now one `portrait_factor` in `view_state.py` read by both callers instead of written twice, and the seven call sites previously patched to `fit_camera=False` one at a time are gone with the default. 0 of 12 after; `test_camera_persistence.py` pins both halves. Verified by screenshot: zoom a site, colour a residue, thicken the sticks, add a sphere — the frame is pixel-identical and only the intended changes appear.

* **Four imaging tools get the tour their help was already waiting for** ([help buttons and guided tours](subsystems/gui-help-and-guides.md)). Allow-list **87 → 83**. Colocalization, drift correction, FRC resolution and particle tracking each shipped a `help.md` and no `guide.json`, so this is only the second half — and each tour is written to say what the help page cannot: which control to touch first, and in what order the checks matter.
  **Coloc** puts registration *before* everything, because the van Steensel CCF peaking away from zero makes every coefficient meaningless and nothing downstream says so; then that thresholds decide Manders entirely, that a coefficient needs its randomisation comparison, and that punctate signal should be counted rather than correlated. **FRC** is built on "the split *is* the measurement" — two labels on *different* structures correlate nowhere and the tool then reports your field of view as the resolution, which is a number rather than an error. **Drift** on the reference choice (first frame never accumulates error, previous frame follows non-monotonic wander but sums its mistakes) and on the fact that a wrapped edge strip is meaningless. **Tracking** on `max step` being the entire safety margin — set it from √(4·D·dt), never from what makes tracks look longest — and on the two things about the MSD fit: the localisation-uncertainty offset is not optional (without it the constant lands in D), and only short lags carry information.
  **The static target check had a false negative of its own, and this batch found it.** Only a *section* answers `{"key": …}` at run time, and a section is what carries a `type` — but `_collect_view_names` took **every** `key` in the view spec, including table columns, plot series and legend entries. So `{"key": "correlation"}` passed the guard by matching an FRC **table column**, and resolved to nothing in the actual window. Four targets slipped through in a single batch this way; two the tour harness caught and two it did not. The collector now requires a sibling `type`, and re-running it flagged all four at once — each then repointed at the real section (`{"title": "FRC"}`, `{"title": "Drift trace"}`, `{"title": "MSD"}`, `{"title": "Coefficients"}`).
  That is the third time a check passed while the window was wrong, and the pattern is the same each time: the guard verifies a *name exists somewhere in the spec*, and only the render verifies it resolves to the thing the reader is looking at.
  Suites: 74(+9 skipped); all four tours walk clean (5, 5, 6 and 6 steps).

* **Synthetic decay and time-resolved anisotropy get a `?` and a tour** ([help buttons and guided tours](subsystems/gui-help-and-guides.md)). Allow-list **89 → 87**.
  **Synthetic decay** is the third known-answer tour, and its help is built on the confusion that most often makes a published lifetime wrong: the `a` column holds **pre-exponential amplitudes**, proportional to the *number of molecules*, not to the light each contributes. The tour points at the two default rows and says what they actually are — amplitude-equal at 1.2 and 4.0 ns is **23 % / 77 %** of the photons, not 50/50. It also names the window trap (256 × 0.032 ns = 8.2 ns holds a 4 ns component barely twice over, and the evidence for a slow component *is* the tail that gets truncated), and why switching shot noise off is right for checking an implementation and wrong for anything about uncertainty.
  **Anisotropy** is the wizard, and its help is about the corrections between "two measured decays" and "an anisotropy", none of which announces itself in the fit statistic: g multiplies I_VH throughout so it scales r(t) **as a whole**; l1/l2 compress the measured anisotropy toward zero on a high-NA objective; and background is *unpolarised*, so it pulls the VV/VH ratio toward 1 — toward zero anisotropy — worst in the tail where slow rotation lives. The check to run first is that r₀ is at or below 0.4: above it is not a discovery, it is a correction that is wrong.
  **A fifth silent-degradation mode, and the most self-contradicting yet.** An AutoForm wizard is a nav list driving a `QStackedWidget`, and the **list** is what updates the page, the title and the subtitle together. `_reveal` was setting the stack, so the anisotropy wizard showed its g-factor fields under the heading **"Welcome"** — a window disagreeing with itself, which a reader can only interpret as a bug in the tool. It now selects the row. Regression test builds the same shape (nav list + stack + heading) and asserts the heading followed.
  Suites: 102(+9 skipped) across the four guards; both tours walk clean (6 steps each); ruff findings unchanged from HEAD.

* **The FCS group is finished: the confocal calculator and the curve merger** ([help buttons and guided tours](subsystems/gui-help-and-guides.md)). Allow-list **91 → 89**. Both are **wizard** plugins whose `entrypoints.gui` names `wizard.py` at the package root, so their help files sit beside that module rather than under `gui/`.
  Neither had a toolbar, so each grew a borderless hairline one. For the merger — a `QWizard`, whose button box is reserved for navigation — the strip is inserted at index 0 of the *page's* layout while the tour host stays the **wizard**, so the spotlight still covers the whole window; `owner=type(self)` anchors the resource lookup at the plugin rather than beside the shared wizard-page class it embeds.
  The **calculator** help is built around the fact that decides its numbers: FCS measures τ, not D, and the conversion needs a beam waist that comes from a calibration dye. The error does not propagate evenly — rₕ goes as 1/D so a 10 % calibration error stays 10 %, but V_eff goes as **w_xy³** so the same error is **33 %**, and concentration inherits that whole cube. S is the other half of V_eff, linear in it, typically 3–6 and *poorly determined by a fit* because the axial dimension barely shows in the curve. And Stokes–Einstein's rₕ is the radius of the sphere that would diffuse this way, not the molecule's size, which is what the ellipsoid/cylinder models exist to correct.
  The **merger** help is about which curves belong in the average at all. Averaging is point-by-point in lag, which is right only if every curve measures the same thing: G(0) = 1/N, so averaging across concentrations gives the mean of the reciprocals rather than a concentration anyone can quote, and a focus that drifted between runs broadens the merged decay past anything in the sample. One aggregate can move the whole mean — G is normalised by the *square* of the mean intensity — which is exactly why the tool has per-curve checkboxes and shows count rates and duration beside every file.
  **A fourth silent-degradation mode in the tour, again found only in the render.** When a tall bubble, a short window and a full-width target leave *no* candidate position clear of the target, some overlap is unavoidable — and minimum overlap alone then picks arbitrarily among near-equal choices. On the calculator it picked the half holding the dye combo the step was explaining. `_place` now buckets the overlap area and breaks the tie toward the **bottom right**, because a form fills left to right and top to bottom: the label, the editor and the first control all live at the target's top left, so that corner is what must survive. Regression test with a 420×550 bubble against a full-width row in an 800-tall window.
  Suites: 79(+8 skipped) across the three guards; both tours walk clean (7 and 5 steps); ruff findings identical to HEAD on every file touched.

* **The framing correction ran on a window that did not exist** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). Five tests in `test_camera_framing.py` were red at HEAD, every one by a factor of **exactly 30**. `scene_width()` subtracts the internal panel's 220-pixel column and clamps the remainder to 1, so a never-laid-out `MolView` (100x30) reported an aspect of **1/30** — and PyMOL's portrait correction, given a window "thirty times taller than wide", put the camera thirty times too far away. `_aspect()` now returns 1.0 below a 16-pixel viewport: an aspect measured off a one-pixel column is not a measurement, and there is nothing to correct until there is a window. Two guardrail tests, one for each direction — the unlaid-out case frames square, a genuine 400x900 portrait still corrects. Found while running the suite for the polar-contact work; unrelated to it, fixed in the same change.

* **Polar contacts in ChiMOL: `distance ... mode=2`** ([PyMOL parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md)). One missing piece was behind three visible symptoms: `preset technical` and `preset ligands` both reported drawing no polar contacts, and the object menu's **A ▸ find** submenu was disabled outright. `chimol/analysis/hbonds.py` transcribes `ObjectMoleculeTestHBond`, `FindBestDonorH`, `GetCheckHBond`, `GetAvgHBondVector` and `CoordSetFindOpenValenceVector`.
  **The cutoff is a curve, not a number** — the donor-acceptor limit slides with the A-D-H angle from `h_bond_cutoff_center` (3.6 Å head-on) to `h_bond_cutoff_edge` (3.2 Å at 63°), and the two names read backwards from what they do. Two more details invisible without the C++: the virtual hydrogen sits at **1.0 Å**, not the real X-H bond length (`FindBestDonorH` adds a *unit* vector), and an atom with no neighbours aims its hydrogen **straight at the acceptor**, which is how PyMOL finds water-mediated contacts in a hydrogen-less PDB rather than a bug to fix.
  Donors and acceptors need bond orders a PDB does not carry. PyMOL fills that with a hard-coded double-bond table for standard residues plus valence arithmetic for the rest; chimol already had the equivalent of the first in the `h_add` residue template, so a templated atom is typed from it (which is what keeps a backbone carbonyl an acceptor and not a donor) and an untemplated one from expected valence with geometry read off its bond angles. **Measured against reality**: on the fully hydrogenated `hGBP1_closed.pdb`, asking with and without hydrogens gives 735 vs 803 contacts sharing 729 pairs — **99.2 % recall** with every hydrogen invented. On 148L, 234 contacts in 0.02 s, over 40 of them the i→i−4 bonds that define an α-helix. One deliberate deviation: PyMOL invents an amide hydrogen for **proline**, which has none.
  With it: `distance` gained PyMOL's full signature and modes 0–4 (all pairs / bonded / polar / exclusion / centroids) with `label`/`quiet`/`reset`; measurements became multi-segment and **dashed** (`dash_length`/`dash_gap`/`dash_width`/`dash_color`); the **A ▸ find ▸ polar contacts** submenu is transcribed from `menu.py::polar`, with halogen/salt-bridge/π left visible-and-disabled rather than dropped. **55 → 68 registered settings**, every one read by code. 20 new tests in `test_hbonds.py`; verified in a real GL window, not offscreen — the first pass drew 1-pixel dashes because `dash_width` was registered and read by nothing, which only the screenshot showed.

* **`.native` is the other way past the chiplot seam, and now it is guarded** ([chiplot](subsystems/chiplot.md)). An `import pyqtgraph` is loud; `Plot.native` is not. It hands back the renderer object directly, so a call site is exactly as coupled as an importer while `pyqtgraph_import_allowlist.txt` sees nothing at all. `test/test_pyqtgraph_seam.py` gained two checks against a second **shrinking** list, `test/chiplot_native_allowlist.txt`, seeded with the **12** files that do it.
  **Most of them are not gaps, which is the finding.** Each was written with a comment calling itself a migration gap — and that is how an assumption survives being wrong. `fcs_lfcs_sim` reached through `.native` to call `enableAutoSIPrefix(False)`; `Plot.set_si_prefix(x=False)` had existed the whole time. Ported in this change, so the list starts at 12 rather than 13. Two more verbs cover much of the rest: `set_axis_visible` for `hideAxis`, `set_tick_spacing` for `getAxis(…).setTickSpacing`.
  What is *genuinely* missing is now written down as an ordered worklist in the concept — axis styling (pen/text colour, height, tick-text offset; 3 consumers), curve performance (`setDownsampling`/`setClipToView`; 2), handle click-signal and export-hint, scene→data coordinates, custom tick labels — so the next porter adds an API rather than reaching past the seam again. **No chiplot API was added here**: another instance holds `canvas.py` and both backends with staged work, and adding verbs underneath that would be worse than waiting.
  The guard strips `#` comments before matching, deliberately: naming the escape hatch in the comment that explains a port *away* from it is not reaching through it, and a guard that cannot tell the difference punishes documenting the fix.
  **The rule this serves:** legacy plotting you walk past is legacy you own — a change that touches one of these files ports it in the same change and strikes the line, rather than noting it. That is what keeps a shrinking list shrinking, and it is the same shape that has been driving the import list from 76 to 15.

* **The lifetime-FCS simulator gets a `?` and a known-answer tour** ([help buttons and guided tours](subsystems/gui-help-and-guides.md)). Allow-list **92 → 91**. Like 2D-FLCS it needs no data of the user's, and every number the tour quotes follows from the defaults: τ_D = w₀²/(4·D) with w₀ = 0.3 µm puts the two species at **2.8 µs** and **45 µs** before anything is pressed.
  The tour is built around the one number that decides whether a filtered curve means anything — the **filter condition number**, printed after every run. Filtered FCS adds no information; it redistributes it, and the price is noise, so the ten-second experiment the tour asks for is to bring τ₂ toward τ₁, re-run, and watch the condition number climb while the curves keep looking like correlation curves. It also names the trap that transfers to real data: a cross-correlation is not automatically exchange, because imperfect filters leak one species into the other's channel — leakage mimics the autocorrelation, exchange is anti-correlated on its own timescale.
  The tool is a plain `QWidget` with no toolbar, so it grew a hairline `QToolBar` for the pair rather than letting the buttons land beside the plot. Suites: 61(+7 skipped) across both seam guards; tour walks clean (7 steps, nothing unresolved, nothing scrolled); ruff clean.

* **2D-FLCS gets a `?` and a tour that walks on its own simulator** ([help buttons and guided tours](subsystems/gui-help-and-guides.md), [filtered FCS](../docs/concepts/filtered_fcs.md)). Allow-list **93 → 92**. The tool's own `FlcHelpDialog` — an HTML literal plus CLI `--help` output — is deleted for `gui/help.md` behind the shared `?`, the third such dialog to go after BVA's and H2MM's.
  The tour needs **no data of the user's**: the plugin's *Simulator* panel generates a two-state exchanging stream whose answer is arithmetic, so the tour states it before pressing Run — τ = 1 and 3 ns with k₁₂ = 30 s⁻¹, k₂₁ = 10 s⁻¹ gives equilibrium populations **0.25/0.75** and a relaxation time **1/(k₁₂+k₂₁) = 25 ms**. The default lag of 1 ms is then the lesson rather than a mis-setting: at 1/25 of the exchange time the map is nearly pure diagonal, which is the correct answer to the question that lag asks. That is the shape to copy — `fcs_lfcs_sim` and `synthetic_decay` can carry it too.
  **A third silent-degradation mode, found the same way as the first two — by looking.** An AutoForm `panel` is a `CollapsibleBox`, and a form of any size folds most of them. A step targeting a control inside a folded panel still *resolves* — the widget has a real geometry, it is simply not drawn — so the guardrail passes, the harness reports `unresolved=[]`, and the spotlight lands on a header bar elsewhere in the column. The first render of this tour put "the answer, before you press anything" next to an empty 20-pixel box. `GuidedTour._reveal` now expands the panel, **and suspends its `auto_fold`**: that setting folds a box when the pointer *leaves* it, and during a tour the pointer is never on it, so a panel opened without that would shut again mid-step. Restored in `stop()`. Regression test verified to fail without the fix.
  **Not ours, recorded rather than chased:** closing this tool prints a pyqtgraph teardown traceback (`ViewBox.forgetView` → a `ViewBoxMenu` whose combo box Qt already deleted). Attributed by disabling the new unfold entirely and walking the tour again — still 2 occurrences; the tour's extra `processEvents` only raises it to 4. H2MM does not reproduce it. See [known issues](references/known-issues.md).
  Suites: 12 (`test_guided_tour`) + 53(+7 skipped) (`test_plugin_help_guide_seam`) + 24(+6 skipped) (`flc_2d`), green; ruff clean. **Method note:** the `flc_2d` suite fails three tests with `RuntimeError: Cannot set NUMBA_NUM_THREADS ... (currently have 7, trying to set 8)` when another instance's suite is running concurrently — pin `NUMBA_NUM_THREADS` to reproduce a clean run, and do not read that failure as a code defect.

* **A `?` and a **Guide** for any tool, and the first twelve tours** ([help buttons and guided tours](subsystems/gui-help-and-guides.md)). Both used to live on `ChisurfDockTool`, which made them a feature of a base class rather than of ChiSurf: roughly thirty tools built on a plain `QMainWindow`/`QWidget` or on `NavigationPanelTool` had no seam at all. They now live in `chisurf/gui/widgets/tools/help_guide.py` as a mixin plus a free function, with three ways in — a plugin that ships `help.md` and `guide.json` beside the module its `entrypoints.gui` names gets both buttons and **changes no code**.
  Enforced by `test/test_plugin_help_guide_seam.py` against a **shrinking** `test/plugin_help_guide_allowlist.txt`, in the spirit of the [chiplot](subsystems/chiplot.md) migration: **105 → 93** of 109 GUI plugins. Presence is not enough — a guide needs three steps, a title and text on each, at least one `await`, and every `attr`/`key` target must exist in the view spec; a help page must clear a minimum length and **every relative link must resolve**, because the modal routes them to the documentation browser and a dead one is only found by clicking it.
  Twelve tours written with real content: burst analysis, accurate FRET, burst GS, burst selection, decay analysis, TTTR Tools, FCS filter calculator, burst background, burst IRF & background, and now **2CDE, BVA and H2MM**. BVA and H2MM each carried their help as an HTML literal plus CLI `--help` output inside a bespoke `HelpDialog`; both are deleted for `help.md` behind the shared `?`.
  **The failure mode this is built against:** a step whose target does not resolve is shown **centred rather than skipped**, so a whole tour can look authored and point at nothing, and no construction test can see the difference. Hence `build_tools/dev_utils/check_plugin_guide.py`, which walks a tour headlessly and checks the three things no unit test can — the buttons exist, every target resolves, and no step is **cut off mid-sentence** (the bubble did that silently for as long as the feature existed, with the buttons drawn neatly underneath). 15/16 tours clean; `PSFCalculator` aborts on construction under the offscreen platform for OpenGL reasons that predate this work.
  **Two GUI defects found by looking at the PNGs, not by reasoning.** (1) *A resolved target is not a visible one.* A `DockArea` tab closed with `close_mode="hide"` stays in the registry, so a `{"tab": …}` step still resolved — to a hidden page carrying the geometry it had when it was closed. The harness reported `unresolved=[]` while the spotlight sat on a rectangle of unrelated panel; only the image showed it. `_resolve_tab` now calls `DockArea.showTab` first. (2) *Restoring that dock put it in the wrong place.* `showTab` asked `find_main_tab_widget`, which returned whichever stack `findChildren` yielded first — **including one `deleteLater`-ed by a layout rebuild but not yet destroyed**, so a settings page rendered at its last standalone size *on top of* the real docks. `find_main_tab_widget` now skips anything outside the layout tree, and `hideTab` records the stack a page came from so `showTab` puts it back there. Three regression tests, each verified to fail without its fix.
  **Method note, worth the paragraph.** The BVA symptom looked like a broken authored layout — the *Channel Definitions* dock was simply not there. It was not: `CHISURF_SETTINGS_DIR` does **not** cover tools that persist through `QSettings("chisurf", "<Tool>")`, which read `~/Library/Preferences/com.chisurf.<Tool>.plist` regardless, so the headless render inherited a tab closed in the user's own session. Neither `HOME=` nor `QSettings.setDefaultFormat(IniFormat)` redirects that on macOS. Applying the default explicitly — `area.set_layout_state(BVATool._default_dock_layout())` — proved the authored layout correct and moved the search to where the bug actually was.
  Also fixed in passing: `test/gui/settings/test_qt_widgets_serialization.py` was **red at HEAD** (three `NameError`s from a class renamed out from under its call sites), and once named correctly, one test asserted a `to_dict` that "fails without `skip_qt_widgets`" — which it has not done for some time. It does not raise; it warns and returns the live `QSpinBox`, so the dict claims to hold only elementary types while holding a widget and the failure surfaces later at the YAML dump. The test now states that.
  Suites: 17 (`test_dock_area`) + 11 (`test_guided_tour`) + 50(+7 skipped) (`test_plugin_help_guide_seam`) + 3 (`test_qt_widgets_serialization`) + 6 (`test_chisurf_dock_tool`) + 25 (burst BVA/H2MM/2CDE plugin suites) — all green. No new ruff findings in any file touched.
  **Not committed: `chisurf/gui/widgets/navigation.py`.** Another instance holds staged work there, interleaved with the `HelpGuideMixin` wiring, so the two `NavigationPanelTool` shells (decay analysis, TTTR Tools) ship both files and show no buttons yet. That is the first thing to pick up; see the concept.

* **The detection profile becomes a fittable object, not a hard-coded Gaussian:
  [PRD-76](prds/prd-76.md) registered.** ([PRDs](prds/index.md))
  Saturation FCS builds its excitation profile from `_gaussian_psf` and derives
  the peak excitation rate from the *Gaussian* peak flux density
  `2 Phi/(pi w0^2)` — so "support another PSF shape" is not a parameter change,
  it is a seam that does not exist yet. The PRD specifies that seam
  (`DetectionProfile`: evaluate on `(r, z)`, own convergent grid, focal-area
  integral, `V_0`, optional analytic `g_diff`) plus six implementations —
  Gaussian, Gaussian beam, the Enderlein Gauss–Lorentz MDF already in
  `enderlein.py`, a diffraction PSF from the optics engine behind the PSF
  calculator, a measured bead-scan profile, and a **fittable Gaussian-sum
  basis** — and then uses it: a **power series fitted globally** recovers the
  real profile, because saturation flattens the profile at a rate set by its
  fall-off, so `V_eff(P)`, `tau_D(P)` and `CPM(P)` together measure the shape.
  Named because it fails silently: reusing `excitation_rate_peak` with a
  non-Gaussian profile still fits the curve and still returns rate constants —
  scaled by a shape-dependent factor. Also recorded as *not identifiable*: a
  single curve can never yield a profile (shape trades against `tau_D` and `N`),
  and even a series leaves `sigma_abs * P` degenerate with `w_r`, so an absolute
  `V_eff` requires an anchor (known `D`, known extinction, or a two-focus
  separation) rather than a number that restates the assumed cross-section.
  **Scoping correction (§3.0):** the seam is small, because every profile in the
  list is *cylindrically symmetric* and the expensive integration already
  assumes only that — `fcs_numerical_g_diff` takes a profile **array** and says
  so ("arbitrary axially symmetric emission profiles"); the Hankel quadrature,
  the axial `rfft` with its mirror weights, the Parseval-exact amplitude, the
  separable propagator and the two-channel path are all shape-blind. What is
  Gaussian is a short list of scalars and defaults around it: `_gaussian_psf`,
  the peak flux density, `V_0 = pi^1.5 w0^2 z0`, the five-waist grid, and — less
  obviously — the **k-space** cut `kr_max = 30/r[-1]`, tuned to truncate a
  *Gaussian* spectrum at 1e-4, which a diffraction ring or a narrow fitted core
  overruns. Consequences now written into the PRD: `grid()` and `quadrature()`
  belong to the profile, convergence must be shown in both spaces (the axial FFT
  is periodic, so a Lorentzian wing wraps rather than vanishing), the cached
  Hankel matrix keys on the grid and not the profile — which is what makes a
  shape fit affordable, provided the grid is pinned rather than chased per
  iteration — and a displaced two-focus geometry stays inside the same `m = 0`
  quadrature as a `J0(k_r d)` weight instead of needing a 3-D transform. Editing
  `fcs_numerical_g_diff` is now a stated sign the seam was drawn in the wrong
  place.

* **A session now has to leave a resume point, and OKF is where it goes.**
  ([change tracking](workflows/change-tracking.md),
  [CLAUDE.md reference](references/claude-md.md))
  The loop said to append to this log and stopped there — but the log records
  *what happened*, newest-first by date, and cannot answer "what next" without
  reading every entry and inferring. The chimol round proved the cost: the most
  useful thing measured (which of PyMOL's 735 unregistered settings are actually
  *used*) existed only in an agent's private notes, which the next session cannot
  read. Step 7 of the loop is now **leave a resume point** — a "Where to pick
  this up" section at the *top* of the concept that owns the area, before the
  findings, so a cold reader hits the open front before the history. What makes
  an entry useful rather than a topic name is spelled out: the measurement **and
  how to re-derive it including the trap in taking it**, what a gap actually
  *blocks* (one missing piece often explains several symptoms, and naming that is
  what orders the list), and approaches **tried and reverted** with why, so they
  are not repeated. Worked example:
  [chimol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md).
  Also recorded, because it silently undermines every rule stated there:
  **`CLAUDE.md` is gitignored**, so it is per-checkout and not a durable record.
  Each of its working-practice rules now has a named owning concept in a table in
  [references/claude-md.md](references/claude-md.md); a rule added there without
  one is lost the next time the file is regenerated.

* **A rebuild was stealing the camera, and side chains now grow out of the
  ribbon.** ([chimol parity](plugins/pymol-parity.md),
  [molecular viewer guide](../docs/guides/44_molecular_viewer.md))
  `cartoon_side_chain_helper` is transcribed from `SideChainHelper.cpp` into
  `analysis/side_chain_helper.py` — the setting that makes the commonest figure
  in structural biology (a cartoon with sticks on a few residues) readable, by
  dropping the backbone bonds a cartoon already covers. It is a **bond filter,
  not an atom filter**: the atoms stay in the model and stay pickable. Kept:
  `CA-CB`, which the side chain hangs from; **proline** keeps its `N-CA` because
  its ring needs it; an atom at the edge of a cartoon segment keeps its backbone
  bonds so the sticks still reach the ribbon. Measured on 148L residues 20–26,
  62 stick bonds become 35 and the 27 dropped are exactly 7 `N-CA`, 7 `CA-C`,
  7 `C-O`, 6 `C-N`. The presets set it for real now instead of reporting it as
  skipped. The first cut was a per-bond Python loop — invisible at 1 000 bonds,
  **1.3 s at 500 000**, and it runs on every rebuild; every test in the rule is
  on the two endpoints, so it vectorises to gathered boolean arrays for the same
  answer at **332 ms, 4× faster**. Not tuned further: the filter runs *after*
  the sticks mask, so its input is the scoped bond list.
  **A camera defect was found by photographing that setting** and is recorded,
  not fixed: the framing kept resetting between the off and on shots, because
  `_update_view` refits the camera on *every* rebuild — and a rebuild is what
  colouring, a representation change, a label and every `set` all trigger.
  Measured: `zoom resi 20-26` puts the camera at 1.26 and the next `set` of
  anything puts it back to 5.0. Flipping the default was tried and **reverted**:
